==History==

===Early history===
The site is ancient; "hurst" is the [[Saxons|Saxon]] term for an enclosed wood. [[Nigel Nicolson]], in his 1964 guide, ''Sissinghurst Castle: An Illustrated History'', records the earliest owners as the de Saxinhersts.{{efn|Nicolson notes that "the spelling of the name fluctuat(es) at the will of the scribe". The brief early records of the site use Saxinherst, Saxingherste and Saxenhurst.{{sfn|Nicolson|1964|p=4}} Adam Nicolson suggests that the name derives from, or is the origin of, Sissinghurst, perhaps meaning "the wood of the Saxons".{{sfn|Nicolson|2008b|p=36}}}} Stephen de Saxinherst is named in an 1180 charter about the nearby [[Combwell Priory]]. At the end of the 13th century the estate had passed, through marriage, to the de Berhams.{{sfn|Nicolson|1964|pp=4–5}} Nicolson suggested that the de Berhams constructed a moated house in stone, of an appearance similar to that of [[Ightham Mote]], which was later replaced by a brick manor.{{sfn|Nicolson|1964|pp=5–6}} More recent studies, including those of Nicolson's son, [[Adam Nicolson|Adam]], cast doubt on the existence of an earlier stone manor, suggesting instead that the brick house, or perhaps a timber construction of a slightly earlier date, occupying the corner of the orchard nearest the moat, was the earliest house on the site.{{sfn|Nicolson|2008|pp=173–174}} [[Edward I]] is reputed to have stayed at this house in 1305.{{sfn|Nicolson|1964|p=5}}

===Rise, decline, collapse: c. 1490–1930===
[[File:Sissinghurst Castle 10.JPG|thumb|left|upright=1.6|alt=Model of Sissinghurst Castle in 1560. From right to left: gatehouse, tower, brick courtyard, wooden courtyard; moat front and left|Model displayed at Sissinghurst depicting Sir Richard Baker's house circa 1560]]
In 1490 the de Berhams sold the manor of Sissinghurst to Thomas Baker of [[Cranbrook, Kent|Cranbrook]].{{sfn|Nicolson|1964|p=6}} The Bakers were cloth producers and in the following century, through marriage and careers at court and in the law, Thomas's successors greatly expanded their wealth and their estates in Kent and [[Sussex]].{{sfn|Nicolson|2008|pp=171–172}} In the 1530s Sir John Baker, one of [[Henry VIII]]'s [[Privy Council of the United Kingdom|Privy Councillors]], built a new brick gatehouse, the current West Range.{{sfn|Newman|2012|p=544}}{{efn|The construction of new homes on sites adjacent to older houses was a fairly common practice in [[Tudor period|Tudor England]]. Sir John's approach was followed, for example, by the [[Duke of Norfolk]] at [[Kenninghall]].{{sfn|Howard|1987|p=17}}}} In 1554 Sir John's daughter Cecily married Thomas Sackville, 1st Earl of Dorset, creating the earliest connection between the Sackville family and the house.{{sfn|Dennison|2015|p=204}} Sir John's son Richard undertook a massive [[Prodigy house|prodigy expansion]] in the 1560s. The Tower is part of that expansion, and formed the entrance to a very large courtyard house, of which the South Cottage and some walls are the only other remaining fragments.{{sfn|Newman|2012|pp=544–545}} Sir Richard surrounded the mansion with an enclosed {{convert|700|acre|km2|adj=on}} [[Deer park (England)|deer park]] and in August 1573 entertained [[Queen Elizabeth I]] at Sissinghurst.{{sfn|Greeves|2008|p=285}}

After the collapse of the Baker family fortunes following the [[English Civil War|civil war]] (1642–1651), the building declined in importance. [[Horace Walpole]] visited in 1752: "yesterday, after twenty mishaps, we got to Sissinghurst for dinner. There is a park in ruins and a house in ten times greater ruins."{{sfn|Nicolson|1964|p=24}} During the [[Seven Years' War]], it became a prisoner-of-war camp.{{sfn|Nicolson|2008b|p=44}}{{efn|An 18th century painting of the castle at this time was identified as being of Sissinghurst only in 2008. Showing the house before its destruction, it is the most complete record of the house as built by Sir Richard Baker. The painting is reproduced on the inside front cover of Adam Nicolson's book, ''Sissinghurst: an unfinished History''.{{sfn|Nicolson|2008|loc=Preface}}}} The historian [[Edward Gibbon]], then serving in the [[Hampshire]] [[militia]], was stationed there and recorded "the inconceivable dirtiness of the season, the country and the spot".{{sfn|Nicolson|1964|pp=35–36}} It was during its use as a camp for French prisoners that the name Sissinghurst Castle was adopted; although it was never a castle, there is debate as to the extent to which the house was a fortified manor.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.gatehouse-gazetteer.info/English%20sites/1660.html|title=Sissinghurst Castle|work=The Gatehouse Gazetteer Guide|access-date=3 October 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180930231241/http://www.gatehouse-gazetteer.info/English%20sites/1660.html|archive-date=30 September 2018|url-status=live}}</ref> In 2018 an important collection of historical [[graffiti]] drawn by some of the 3,000 prisoners was uncovered beneath 20th-century plaster.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/art/art-seven-years-war-sissinghurst-national-trust-kent-a8328186.html|title=Long lost art of first major global war discovered in Kent|first=David|last=Keys|date=29 April 2018|work=The Independent|access-date=2 November 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181103221709/https://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/art/art-seven-years-war-sissinghurst-national-trust-kent-a8328186.html|archive-date=3 November 2018|url-status=live}}</ref>
Around 1800, the estate was purchased by the [[Sir Horatio Mann, 2nd Baronet|Mann family]]<ref name="parksandgardens.org">{{cite web|url=https://www.parksandgardens.org/places/sissinghurst-castle|title=Sissinghurst Castle|work=Parks & Gardens UK|access-date=4 November 2018}}</ref> and the majority of Sir Richard's [[Elizabethan era|Elizabethan]] house was demolished; the stone and brick were reused in buildings throughout the locality.{{sfn|Nicolson|1964|p=42}} The castle later became a workhouse for the Cranbrook Union, after which it housed farm labourers.{{sfn|Nicolson|2008b|p=45}} In 1928, the castle was put up for sale for a price of £12,000, but attracted no bids for two years.{{sfn|Nicolson|1964|p=44}}

===Vita Sackville-West and Harold Nicolson: 1930–1968===
====Vita Sackville-West====
{{Main|Vita Sackville-West}}
[[File:Sissinghurst Castle (8).JPG|thumb|right|upright|alt=portrait of woman hanging above a fireplace in a wood-panelled room|Sackville-West's portrait by [[Philip de László]] hanging in the Big Room of the West Range]]
Vita Sackville-West, poet, author, and gardener, was born at Knole, about 25 miles from Sissinghurst, on 9 March 1892.{{sfn|Glendinning|2005|p=1}} The great Elizabethan mansion, home of her ancestors but denied to her through [[agnatic primogeniture]],{{sfn|Glendinning|2005|p=9}}{{efn|Although her father [[Lionel Sackville-West, 3rd Baron Sackville|Lionel's]] only child, and a Sackville twice over, through her parents being cousins and her grandfathers being brothers, the practice of inheritance solely through the male line saw Knole pass to her father's brother [[Charles Sackville-West, 4th Baron Sackville|Charles]].{{sfn|Sackville-West|2010|p=232}}}} held enormous importance for her throughout her life.{{sfn|Brown|1998|p=24}}{{sfn|Sackville-West|2010|p=249}}{{efn|The county of Kent, as well as Knole, had significance for Sackville-West. Her epic poem, ''The Land'', includes the lines; "Hear first of the country that shall claim my theme, the Weald of Kent, once forest, and to-day meadow and orchard, garden of fruit and hops, a green, wet country on a bed of clay ..."<ref name="auto4">{{cite web|url=https://gutenberg.ca/ebooks/sackvillewestv-theland/sackvillewestv-theland-00-h.html|title=The Land|last=Sackville-West|first=Vita|work=Project Gutenberg|access-date=24 December 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150328074132/http://www.gutenberg.ca/ebooks/sackvillewestv-theland/sackvillewestv-theland-00-h.html|archive-date=28 March 2015|url-status=live}}</ref>}} Sissinghurst was a substitute for Knole, and she greatly valued its familial connections.{{sfn|Glendinning|2005|p=224}}{{sfn|Brown|1998|p=23}}{{efn|The ''Table of Descent'' set out in her book, ''Knole And The Sackvilles'', records the marriage of [[Thomas Sackville, 1st Earl of Dorset|Thomas Sackville]] to Cecily, daughter of Sir John Baker of Sissinghurst Castle, Cranford, Kent in 1554.{{sfn|Sackville-West|1991|loc=Foreword ix}}}} In 1913 Sackville-West married Harold Nicolson, a diplomat at the start of his career.{{sfn|Sackville-West|2010|p=219}} Their relationship was unconventional, with both pursuing multiple, mainly same-sex, affairs. After breaking with her lover [[Violet Trefusis]] in 1921, Sackville-West became increasingly withdrawn.{{sfn|Nicolson|1990|p=211}} She wrote to her mother that she would like "to live alone in a tower with her books", an ambition she achieved in the tower at Sissinghurst where only her dogs were regularly admitted.{{sfn|Jenkins|2003|p=381}}{{sfn|Rose|2006|p=48}}{{efn|Sackville-West consciously designed Sissinghurst without any guest accommodation, as her dislike of visitors and love of solitude came to be dominant features in her character. Nigel Nicolson recorded his mother's explanation for requiring that he and his brother share a bedroom until they went to university. "If we had a bedroom each and one of us was away [[Sibyl, Lady Colefax|Lady Colefax]] might find out and invite herself for the weekend."{{sfn|Nicolson|1992|p=10}}}}

From 1946 until a few years before her death, Sackville-West wrote a gardening column for ''[[The Observer]]'', in which, although she never referred directly to Sissinghurst,{{sfn|Brown|1985|p=183}} she discussed a wide array of horticultural issues.{{sfn|Brown|1998|p=33}}{{efn|These were subsequently published in four volumes by [[Michael Joseph (publisher)|Michael Joseph]]; ''In your Garden'' (1951), ''In Your Garden Again'' (1953), ''More For Your Garden'' (1955) and ''Even More for Your Garden'' (1958).{{sfn|Raven|2014|p=367}}}} In an article, "Some Flowers", she discussed the challenge of writing effectively about flowers: "I discovered this only when I started to do so. Before ... I found myself losing my temper with the nauseating phraseology ... and sickly vocabulary employed."{{sfn|Hoyles|1994|p=98}} In 1955, in recognition of her achievement at Sissinghurst, "bending some stubborn acres to my will",<ref name="auto4"/> she was awarded the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Veitch Memorial Medal|Veitch Medal]].<ref name="auto1">{{cite web|url=https://historicengland.org.uk/research/inclusive-heritage/womens-history/registered-parks-gardens/vita-sackville-west/|title=Vita Sackville-West and Sissinghurst Castle|author=Historic England|website=historicengland.org.uk|access-date=3 October 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180721162158/https://historicengland.org.uk/research/inclusive-heritage/womens-history/registered-parks-gardens/vita-sackville-west/|archive-date=21 July 2018|url-status=live}}</ref> Her biographer [[Victoria Glendinning]] considers Sissinghurst to be Sackville-West's "one magnificent act of creation".{{sfn|Glendinning|2005|p=302}}

====Harold Nicolson====
{{Main|Harold Nicolson}}
Harold Nicolson, diplomat, author, diarist, and politician, was born in [[Tehran]] on 21 September 1886.{{sfn|Rose|2006|p=2}} Following his father into the diplomatic corps, he served as a junior member of the British delegation at the [[Paris Peace Conference, 1919|Paris Peace Conference]] at the end of the [[First World War]],{{sfn|MacMillan|2001|p=32}} and returned to Iran as Counsellor in 1925.{{sfn|Lees-Milne|1980|p=240}} In 1929 he resigned from the [[Foreign and Commonwealth Office|Foreign Office]]{{sfn|Rose|2006|pp=162–163}} to pursue a career in journalism,{{sfn|Lees-Milne|1980|p=389}} editing the ''[[Londoner's Diary]]'' for [[Lord Beaverbrook]]'s ''[[Evening Standard]]''.{{sfn|Taylor|1972|p=216}} This proved unsuccessful, as did his subsequent political career, which saw him move from [[Oswald Mosley|Oswald Mosley's]] [[New Party (UK)|New Party]]{{sfn|Rose|2006|p=168}} to [[Clement Attlee|Clement Attlee's]] [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour Party]].{{sfn|Rose|2006|p=274}}  Throughout, he maintained a detailed private diary. His entry for 4 April 1930, records, "Vita telephones to say she has seen the ideal house – a place in Kent, near Cranbrook, a sixteenth-century castle".{{sfn|Nicolson|1966|p=44}}

====Building a garden====
{{quote box|width=25em|bgcolor=#c6dbf7|align=right|quote=One might reasonably have hoped to inherit century-old hedges of yew, some gnarled mulberries, a cedar or two, a pleached alley, flagged walls, a mound. Instead there was nothing but weed, rough grass, a shabby eyesore of a greenhouse in the wrong place, broken fencing, wired chicken runs, squalor and slovenly disorder everywhere.|source=–Sackville-West's first impressions of Sissinghurst{{sfn|Jenkins|2003|p=381}}}}

Sackville-West and Nicolson found Sissinghurst in April 1930,{{sfn|Nicolson|1964|p=44}} after [[Dorothy Wellesley, Duchess of Wellington|Dorothy Wellesley]], their near neighbour and a former lover of Sackville-West's, saw the estate for sale.{{sfn|Nicolson|2008b|p=46}} They had become increasingly concerned about encroaching development near their property [[Long Barn]], near [[Sevenoaks]], Kent.{{sfn|Nicolson|2008b|p=46}}{{efn|In 1925, they had considered [[Bodiam Castle]] as an alternative to Long Barn. Their plan was for they and the children each to inhabit one of the four concentric towers.{{sfn|Raven|2014|p=38}} However the price, £30,000, was well beyond their means.{{sfn|Brown|1985|p=107}}}} Their offer on Sissinghurst was accepted on 6 May{{sfn|Nicolson|1966|p=48}} and the castle and the farm around it were bought for £12,375, using only Sackville-West's money rather than Nicolson's.{{sfn|Brown|1985|p=111}}

The property was {{convert|450|acre|km2}} in total.<ref name=acres>{{cite web|url=https://www.anglotopia.net/british-history/great-british-gardens-sissinghurst-castle-garden-visited-garden-england/|title=Great British Gardens: Sissinghurst Castle Garden – The Most Visited Garden in England|first=Jonathan|last=Thomas|work=Anglotopia|date=8 January 2015|access-date=21 December 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181222035745/https://www.anglotopia.net/british-history/great-british-gardens-sissinghurst-castle-garden-visited-garden-england/|archive-date=22 December 2018|url-status=live}}</ref> The house had no electricity, running water, or drains, and the garden was in disarray.{{sfn|Nicolson|2008b|p=46}} Anne Scott-James notes their "planting inheritance" as "a grove of nut-trees, some apple trees, a [[quince]] [and] a tangle of old roses". The physical assets on the site were "four buildings of beautiful mellow brick, part of a moat [and] various fine walls".{{sfn|Scott-James|1974|p=37}} Clearing the ground took almost three years, but by 1939 the garden was largely complete, with the exception of the White Garden. Nicolson was responsible for the design and layout, while Sackville-West, at the head of her team of gardeners, undertook the planting. [[Simon Jenkins]], the architectural writer, describes Nicolson's design as "post-Picturesque, a garden not as an imitation of nature but as imitation of a house", and suggests his thinking was much influenced by [[Lawrence Waterbury Johnston|Lawrence Johnston]]'s garden at [[Hidcote Manor Garden|Hidcote]].{{sfn|Jenkins|2003|p=381}} Sackville-West's approach was plant-centred, within the constraints of her husband's plan, "profusion, even extravagance and exuberance, within confines of the utmost linear severity".<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/gardening/9346537/Vita-Sackville-West-her-gardening-legacy.html|title=Vita Sackville-West: her gardening legacy|first=Matthew|last=Dennison|date=22 June 2012|work=The Telegraph|access-date=31 October 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181101015508/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/gardening/9346537/Vita-Sackville-West-her-gardening-legacy.html|archive-date=1 November 2018|url-status=live}}</ref>

The buildings scattered around the site were converted to become an unconventional home. Part of the long brick gatehouse range from Sir John Baker's construction of c.1533 became the library, or Big Room;{{sfn|Greeves|2008|p=285}} the tower gatehouse dating from Richard Baker's rebuilding in 1560–1570 became Sackville-West's sitting room, study, and sanctuary.{{sfn|Greeves|2008|p=285}} The Priest's House was home to their sons [[Benedict Nicolson|Ben]] and Nigel, and held the family dining room, while the South Cottage housed their bedrooms and Nicolson's writing room.{{sfn|Brown|1998|pp=95–96}}

The garden was first opened to the paying public for two days in mid-1938.{{efn|A young visitor on that first opening recalled being terrified by "the looming giantess in top boots" and annoyed by the "snooty" boys who surveyed the visitors from the tower.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/gardening/open-gardens/9212009/Visiting-gardens-a-national-obsession.html|title=Visiting gardens: a national obsession|first=Ambra|last=Edwards|date=18 April 2012|work=The Telegraph|access-date=6 September 2019}}</ref>}}  Thereafter, the opening hours were gradually increased.{{sfn|Scott-James|1974|p=67}} Despite her love of privacy, Sackville-West came to enjoy greatly her encounters with the visitors, known as "shillingses" on account of the entrance fees they deposited in a bowl at the gate.{{sfn|Raven|2014|p=348}} She described her relationship with them in a 1939 article in the ''[[New Statesman]]'': "between them and myself a particular form of courtesy survives, a gardener's courtesy". Nicolson was less welcoming.{{sfn|Scott-James|1974|p=67}} Sackville-West's ''Observer'' articles raised awareness of the garden; Scott-James records photographic articles in ''[[The Gardeners' Chronicle|Gardening Illustrated]],'' ''[[Vogue (magazine)|Vogue]]'', and ''[[Picture Post]]'', and notes consequently that "increasingly paying visitors poured into Sissinghurst, coming in thousands in the course of a summer".{{sfn|Scott-James|1974|pp=108–109}}

====War and after====
[[File:Statue, Sissinghurst.JPG|thumb|upright=0.8|left|alt=statue on a plinth in front of a green hedge. A youth in classical dress leans against a tree trunk|The statuary at Sissinghurst was not always of the highest quality. [[Anne Scott-James]] describes this one of [[Dionysus]] as looking "particularly depressed".{{sfn|Scott-James|1974|p=66}}{{efn|Anne Scott-James remarks that the Nicolsons' relatively limited means sometimes impacted on their plans. Paths were laid from concrete cast on-site, rather than by using the [[Yorkstone|York stone]] slabs both of them would have preferred, and "most of the statues were picked up in junk shops and are without distinction".{{sfn|Scott-James|1974|pp=65–66}} Adam Nicolson describes the statues, with the exceptions of the pieces inherited from or given by Lady Sackville, as "cheap".{{sfn|Nicolson|2008b|p=46}}}}]]

Nicolson's diary entry for 26 September 1938 records the tense European atmosphere at the time of the [[Munich Agreement|Munich Crisis]]. "They are making the big room at Sissinghurst gas-proof. I know one who will not be there. He will be in his bed minus gas-mask and with all the windows open."{{sfn|Nicolson|1966|p=366}} He drove down to Sissinghurst on the day war was declared, encountering an angry woman who shook her fist at him while declaring that the war was the fault of the rich. He found on his arrival at the castle that the Sackville flag had been lowered from the tower.{{sfn|Tinniswood|2016|pp=368–369}} During the [[Second World War]], Sissinghurst saw much of the [[Battle of Britain]], which was mainly fought over the Weald and the [[English Channel]]. Nicolson's diary entry for 2 September 1940 reads: "a tremendous raid in the morning and the whole upper air buzzes and zooms with the noise of aeroplanes. There are many fights over our sunlight fields".{{sfn|Nicolson|1967|p=110}}{{efn|Although Sissinghurst was undamaged, Knole was bombed in 1944. This prompted Sackville-West into violent reaction. "I mind frightfully, frightfully, frightfully. I always persuade myself that I have finally torn Knole out of my heart, and then the moment anything touches it, every nerve is alive again. I cannot bear to think of Knole wounded. Those filthy Germans! Let us level every town in Germany to the ground! I shan't care."{{sfn|Scott-James|1974|p=99}}}}

In 1956, the [[BBC]] proposed making a television programme at Sissinghurst. Although Sackville-West was in favour, Nicolson was opposed. "I have a vague prejudice against (a) exposing my intimate affections to the public gaze; (b) indulging in private theatricals."{{sfn|Nicolson|1968|p=300}} He later withdrew his objections, but Sackville-West declined the BBC's offer in order to please him.{{sfn|Nicolson|1968|p=300}} In 1959 the American [[CBS]] network broadcast a four-way discussion from the dining room at the Priest's House, between Nicolson, the journalist [[Edward R. Murrow]], and the diplomats [[Charles E. Bohlen|Chip Bohlen]] and [[Clare Boothe Luce]]. Sackville-West intensely disliked the result.{{sfn|Nicolson|1968|pp=373–374}}

Sackville-West died in the first-floor bedroom of the Priest's House on 2 June 1962.{{sfn|Nicolson|1964|p=47}} Nicolson recorded her death in his diary: "Ursula{{efn|Ursula Codrington was Sackville-West's secretary from 1959.{{sfn|Scott-James|1974|p=112}}}} is with Vita. At about 1.5 she observes that Vita is breathing heavily, and then suddenly is silent. She dies without fear or self-reproach. I pick some of her favourite flowers and lay them on her bed".{{sfn|Nicolson|1968|p=415}}{{efn|This entry ends the published collection of Nicolson's diaries, an endeavour begun on 1 January 1930. Although he continued the diary until October 1964, Nigel Nicolson considered the material written after his mother's death to be too personal: "His grief can be imagined but should not be laid bare."{{sfn|Nicolson|1968|p=23}}}} Her death devastated Nicolson and his last years were not happy.{{sfn|Nicolson|1990|pp=216–218}} Giving up his [[Albany (London)|Albany]] apartment in May 1965, he retired to Sissinghurst and thereafter he never stayed anywhere else.{{sfn|Lees-Milne|1981|p=352}} He died of a heart attack in his bedroom at the South Cottage on 1 May 1968.{{sfn|Rose|2006|p=299}}

====Nigel Nicolson====
{{Main|Nigel Nicolson}}
{{quote box|width=25em|bgcolor=#c6dbf7|align=right|quote=Never, never, never! Au grand jamais, jamais. Never, never, never! ... so long as I live no National Trust ... shall have my darling. No, no. Over my corpse or my ashes, not otherwise. It is bad enough to have lost my Knole but they shan't take Sissinghurst from me. That at least is my own. They shan't, they shan't, I won't. They can't make me, I won't. They can't make me. I never would.|source=–Sackville-West's reaction to the suggestion that Sissinghurst might be gifted to the National Trust{{sfn|Nicolson|1968|p=268}}}}

Nigel Nicolson had always been devoted to his father, and admiring of his more distant mother.{{sfn|Nicolson|1990|p=212}} Preserving Sissinghurst was "an act of intense filial duty".{{sfn|Nicolson|2008|p=445}} He had first raised the possibility of giving the house and garden to the National Trust in 1954, but Sackville-West was adamantly opposed.{{sfn|Nicolson|1968|p=268}} After her death in 1962, which saw the castle pass to him although Benedict was the elder son, he began lengthy negotiations to bring about the handover.

The Trust was cautious: it felt that an endowment beyond the Nicolsons' means would be required,{{sfn|Nicolson|2008|p=44}} and it was also unsure that the garden was of sufficient importance to warrant acceptance. [[George Taylor (botanist)|Sir George Taylor]], Chairman of the National Trust's Gardens Committee doubted it was "one of the great gardens of England",{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=18}} and had to be persuaded of its merits by Sackville-West's close friend and one-time lover,{{sfn|Rose|2006|p=83}} the gardener [[Alvilde Lees-Milne]].{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=18}}{{efn|The Trust had, at this time, taken on relatively few gardens. [[Bodnant Garden|Bodnant]] had come in 1949 and [[Nymans]] in 1954. Perhaps the most significant for Sissinghurst had been [[Hidcote Manor Garden|Hidcote]], accepted largely at Sackville-West's urging through her membership of the Trust's Gardens Committee.{{sfn|Brown|1998|p=44}}{{sfn|Brown|1985|p=159}}}}{{efn|Lees-Milne's husband, James Lees-Milne, recorded a conversation with her in his diary entry for 23 June 1972: "A. in the car said we owed more to Harold and Vita than almost any of our older, now dead friends. A. said she owed what gardening credit she now enjoys entirely to Vita who taught her all she knows. I thought of what I owed Harold."{{sfn|Lees-Milne|1994|p=252}}}} Discussions continued until, in April 1967, the castle, garden, and Sissinghurst Farm were finally accepted.{{sfn|Nicolson|2008|p=48}}

Although always intending to transfer Sissinghurst to the Trust, Nigel Nicolson undertook major remodelling at the castle. Unwilling to live in four separate structures – the Big Room, the Tower, the Priest's House, and the South Cottage – he built a substantial family home in the half of the entrance range that stood on the side of the gateway opposite from the library.{{sfn|Nicolson|1964|p=47}} He died at the castle on 23 September 2004.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/news/2004/sep/24/guardianobituaries.books|title=Obituary: Nigel Nicolson|first=Michael|last=de-la-Noy|date=24 September 2004|work=The Guardian|access-date=23 July 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180723212349/https://www.theguardian.com/news/2004/sep/24/guardianobituaries.books|archive-date=23 July 2018|url-status=live}}</ref>

===National Trust: 1967–present===
The National Trust took over the whole of Sissinghurst – its garden, farm, and buildings – in 1967.{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=18}} Since then, the number of visitors has steadily increased. [[Anne Scott-James]],  the author of the first non-Nicolson history of the garden, records 13,200 visitors in 1961, the year of Sackville-West's death, 47,100 in 1967, when the castle passed to the Trust, and 91,584 by 1973.{{sfn|Scott-James|1974|p=124}} It is now among the Trust's most popular properties, receiving nearly 200,000 visitors in 2017.<ref name="auto5">{{cite web|url=http://www.alva.org.uk/details.cfm?p=423|title=Latest Visitor Figures – 2017|work=ALVA-Association of Leading Visitor Attractions|access-date=3 October 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150413023806/http://www.alva.org.uk/details.cfm?p=423|archive-date=13 April 2015|url-status=live}}</ref> Although the increased foot traffic has necessitated the replacement of the grass paths with York paving stones, the entry fees generate considerable income which, under the terms of the handover, can only be expended on Sissinghurst. In 2008, Adam Nicolson described the estate as "better funded than it has been since the 16th century".{{sfn|Nicolson|2008b|p=51}} Major works of reconstruction, such as the restoration of the Tower brickwork, and the cataloguing and conservation of the collection of books in the library, have been made possible by the availability of these funds.{{sfn|Raven|2014|p=357}}

The property has an iconic status in [[LGBTQ culture]]; Adam Nicolson has noted "rivers of lesbians coming through the gate" each spring.<ref name=secateurs/> The castle was one of the sites chosen in 2017 as a focus for the celebration of the LGBTQ history of Trust buildings.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2016/dec/21/national-trust-prepares-to-celebrate-its-gay-history|title=National Trust prepares to celebrate its gay history|first=Maev|last=Kennedy|date=21 December 2016|work=The Guardian|access-date=3 October 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180930193232/https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2016/dec/21/national-trust-prepares-to-celebrate-its-gay-history|archive-date=30 September 2018|url-status=live}}</ref> In the same year, the Trust opened the South Cottage to visitors for the first time.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.kent-life.co.uk/home/south-cottage-opens-at-sissinghurst-castle-garden-1-4850824|title=South Cottage opens at Sissinghurst Castle Garden|first=Sarah|last=Sturt|date=16 January 2017|work=Kent Life|access-date=3 October 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180930193218/http://www.kent-life.co.uk/home/south-cottage-opens-at-sissinghurst-castle-garden-1-4850824|archive-date=30 September 2018|url-status=live}}</ref> {{As of|2019|alt=For 2019|post=,}} the gardens are open to the public daily from 7 March to 31 October.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/place-pages/299/pages/opening-times-calendar|title=Opening Times – Sissinghurst Castle Garden |work=National Trust|access-date=23 February 2019}}</ref> It was ranked 42nd on the list of the Trust's most-visited sites in the 2021–2022 season, with over 150,000 visitors.<ref>{{Cite web |title=National Trust (Annual Report 2022)|url=https://redrocketdigital.co.uk/eBook/14466-National-Trust-Annual-Report-2022/index.html |access-date=21 March 2023|publisher=National Trust}}</ref>

==Architecture and landscape==
===Plan===
[[File:Sissinghurst Castle Gardens - Labelled map.png|thumb|centre|upright=3.0|alt=labelled map of the gardens|Key: A – Priest's House, Erechtheum and White Garden; B – Delos; C – Top Courtyard, West Range and Purple Border; D – Entrance; E – Tower and Lower Courtyard; F – Yew Walk; G – Orchard; H – Rose Garden; I – South Cottage and Cottage Garden; J – Moat Walk and Azaleas; K – Nuttery; L – Herb Garden; M – Lime Walk<br />The top of the map points north-northeast,{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=9}} and the area shown is about {{convert|5|acre|km2}}.<ref name=acres/>]]

===Buildings===
The site is a Grade I [[registered garden]],<ref name="auto6">{{National Heritage List for England|num=1000181|desc=Sissinghurst Castle, Cranbrook|grade=I|access-date=24 January 2019}}</ref> and many other structures within the garden are [[listed building]]s in their own right.<ref name="auto1"/>

====West Range====
[[File:Sissinghurst - entrance range - geograph.org.uk - 188829.jpg|thumb|upright=1.2|right|alt=a long range of brick buildings with a central arch|The West Range]]
The West Range forms part of Sir John Baker's original house of the 1530s.{{sfn|Newman|2012|pp=544–546}}{{efn|The [[National Heritage List for England]] gives a date of 1490, some forty years earlier.<ref name="auto2">{{National Heritage List for England|num=1346285|desc=West Range At Sissinghurst Castle, Cranbrook|grade=I|access-date=24 January 2019}}</ref>}} Sackville-West and Nicolson enlisted architect [[Albert Powys|A.R. Powys]] to help convert the stables into a library, known as the Big Room and containing an important literary collection.{{sfn|Brown|1985|p=122}} For the design of the Big Room, they also employed [[Philip Tilden]].{{efn|In 2017 the Libraries Curator of the National Trust, Mark Purcell, published a book, ''The Country House Library'', which considered the history of such rooms from Roman times to the present. The front cover photograph for the work is of Sackville-West's study at the top of the tower at Sissinghurst.{{sfn|Purcell|2019|loc=cover}}}}{{sfn|Purcell|2019|p=275}} The room as a whole is a recreation of Knole, "Vita's record of her disinheritance".{{sfn|Nicolson|2008b|p=12}} Powys provided most of the architectural input into the conversion of the buildings at Sissinghurst, including the Priest's House and the South Cottage, as well as occasionally advising on elements of the design of the gardens.{{sfn|Brown|1998|p=30}}{{efn|Powys' advice was not always welcomed. A design for a door in the Priest's House evoked a forthright response from Sackville-West. "It's simply bloody, all studded with nails, Ye Olde Tea Shoppe with a vengeance!"{{sfn|Brown|1985|p=123}}}}{{efn|The library contains a portrait of Sackville-West from 1910 by [[Philip de László]]. Sackville-West's mother, [[Victoria Sackville-West, Baroness Sackville|Lady Sackville]] asked de László, "Do you not think that you owe it to your art and to her beauty to paint her without a fee?" Sackville-West disliked the painting and it was kept in an attic until the Trust placed it in the Big Room after taking ownership of Sissinghurst.{{sfn|Nicolson|2008b|p=12}}}}

The range is of brick and of two storeys, with attics and decorated gables and chimneys. The wing to the south was converted into a family home by Nigel Nicolson. The [[coat of arms]] of the [[Baron Carnock|Carnocks]] above the entrance archway was brought to Sissinghurst by Nicolson.<ref name="auto2"/>{{efn|Nicolson's father [[Arthur Nicolson, 1st Baron Carnock|Arthur]] was made 1st [[Baron Carnock]] in 1916.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/r/C12027|title=Sir Arthur Nicholson, 1st Baron Carnock: Papers|work=The National Archives|access-date=7 October 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181007112002/http://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/r/C12027|archive-date=7 October 2018|url-status=live}}</ref> Harold's diary entry for 20 April 1933 records, "Vita and the boys pick me up and we motor down to Sissinghurst. Arrive soon after eight. The arms are on the porch".{{sfn|Nicolson|1966|p=147}} The arms are dated 1548.{{sfn|Newman|2012|pp=544–546}}}} The West Range has a Grade I listing.<ref name="auto2"/>

====Tower====
[[File:Sissinghurst 2022-04-27f.jpg|thumb|left|upright|alt=a high tower of red brick with two pyramid roofs and a flag flying|The Tower]]
The Tower is of brick and was the entrance to the [[cour d'honneur]] of the 1560s rebuilding.{{sfn|Newman|2012|pp=544–546}} Of four storeys, it has recessed staircase turrets to each side, creating what the architectural historian [[Mark Girouard]] described as an "extraordinarily slender and elegant" appearance.{{sfn|Girouard|2009|p=97}} The courtyard was open on the tower side, its three facades containing seven [[Classical architecture|classical]] doorways. Girouard notes Horace Walpole's observation of 1752, "perfect and very beautiful".{{sfn|Girouard|2009|p=171}} Such an arrangement of a three-sided courtyard with a prominent gatehouse set some way in front became popular from Elizabethan times, similar examples being [[Rushton Hall]] and the original [[Lanhydrock]].{{sfn|Girouard|2009|p=80}}

The Tower was Sackville-West's sanctum; her study was out of bounds to all but her dogs and a small number of guests by invitation.{{sfn|Brown|1998|p=54}}{{efn|Nigel Nicolson recalled that, at her death, he had only been up to the tower room on about six occasions in 30 years.{{sfn|Raven|2014|p=45}}}} Her writing room is maintained largely as it was at the time of her death. Nigel Nicolson records his discovery in the Tower of his mother's manuscript describing her affair with Violet Trefusis. This went on to form the basis of his book ''Portrait of a Marriage''.{{sfn|Nicolson|1990|p=7}}{{efn|Publication of the details of the Sackville-West/Nicolson marriage was controversial and Nigel Nicolson sustained much criticism; the actor [[Dirk Bogarde]] wrote, "Just when you think it is safe to stick your head above the parapet to get a gulp of air, bang! crash! wallop! and once more one is cowed by salvoes of the dreaded V-3s, Vita, Violet and Virginia . . . Why does an elderly gentleman see fit to rake through the ashes of his parents' love and expose their very private thoughts to all and sundry, for, as Vita would have said, 'the delectation of the common herd'?"<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/obituaries/1472457/Nigel-Nicolson.html|title=Obituary: Nigel Nicolson|date=24 September 2004|work=The Telegraph|access-date=23 July 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180702182224/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/obituaries/1472457/Nigel-Nicolson.html|archive-date=2 July 2018|url-status=live}}</ref> [[Bernard Levin]]'s ''[[The Observer|Observer]]'' review was more coruscating still; "(Nicolson) tells us that when he found the diary he 'read it through to the end without stirring from her table.' He should then have put it in the fire".<ref>{{cite news |last=Levin|first=Bernard |date=28 October 1973|title=Marriage à la mode |work= The Observer}}</ref> Harold Nicolson's biographer James Lees-Milne recorded a lunch with Nigel Nicolson and a subsequent discussion with two other friends in his diary entry for 14 March 1973; "Both think Nigel ought not to cash in on his parents' love life. I am not sure. I think the book, which is going to be ''the'' book of 1973, will enhance [Vita's] ultimate reputation, though not immediately".{{sfn|Lees-Milne|1997|p=22}}}} The clock, below the Tower parapet, was installed in 1949.{{sfn|Brown|1985|p=200}} A plaque is affixed to the arch of the Tower;{{sfn|Nicolson|2008b|p=30}} the words were chosen by Harold Nicolson: "Here lived V. Sackville-West who made this garden". Nigel Nicolson always felt that the memorial failed to acknowledge his father's contribution.{{sfn|Raven|2014|pp=31–34}} The Tower has a Grade I listing.<ref>{{National Heritage List for England|num=1084163|desc=Tower and Walls 30 yards East of the West Range at Sissinghurst Castle, Cranbrook|grade=I|access-date=24 January 2019}}</ref>

====Priest's House====
[[File:Priest House, Sissinghurst Castle (geograph 5353564).jpg|thumb|right|alt=a view of a cottage in a garden full of flowers|The Priest's House]]
The architectural historian [[John Newman (architectural historian)|John Newman]] suggests that this building was a "viewing pavilion or lodge".{{sfn|Newman|2012|pp=544–546}} Its name derives from the tradition that it was used to house a Catholic priest, the Baker family having been Catholic adherents.{{sfn|Nicolson|2008b|p=42}} Sackville-West and Nicolson converted the cottage to provide accommodation for their sons, and the family kitchen and dining room. Of red brick and two storeys, Historic England suggests that the building may originally have been attached to Sir Richard Baker's 1560s house<ref>
{{National Heritage List for England|num=1346286|desc=The Priest's House at Sissinghurst Castle, Cranbrook|grade=II*|access-date=24 January 2019}}</ref> but Newman disagrees.{{sfn|Newman|2012|pp=544–546}}

====South Cottage====
This building formed the southeast corner of the courtyard enclosure buildings.{{sfn|Newman|2012|pp=544–546}} It was restored by Beale & Son, builders from [[Royal Tunbridge Wells|Tunbridge Wells]], and provided the pair with separate bedrooms, a shared sitting room, and Nicolson's writing room.{{sfn|Brown|1998|pp=95–96}} His diary entry for 20 April 1933 records: "My new wing has been done. The sitting room is lovely ... My bedroom, [[Flush toilet|w.c.]] and bathroom are divine".{{sfn|Nicolson|1966|p=147}} Of two storeys in red brick, with an extension dating from the 1930s, South Cottage has a Grade II* listing.<ref>{{National Heritage List for England|num=1084164|desc=The South Cottage, Cranbrook|grade=II*|access-date=24 January 2019}}</ref>

===Gardens===
[[File:Sissinghurst 2022-04-27l.jpg|thumb|left|upright|alt=a view of an arch in a pink brick wall with a path leading to a statue|An axial walk]]
Although the estate as a whole is {{convert|450|acre|km2}}, the gardens themselves occupy only {{convert|5|acre|km2}}.<ref name=acres/> Anne Scott-James sets out the principles of the design: "a garden of formal structure, of a private and secret nature, truly English in character, and plant[ed] with romantic profusion".{{sfn|Scott-James|1974|p=38}} As gardeners and landscapers, both Sackville-West and Nicolson were amateurs.{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=15}} Nicolson largely undertook the design and Sackville-West the planting. The landscape is designed as a series of "garden rooms", each with a different character of colour or theme, the enclosures being high clipped hedges and pink brick walls.{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=12}} The rooms and "doors" are so arranged as to offer glimpses into other parts of the garden.

Sackville-West described the overall design: "a combination of long axial walks, usually with terminal points, and the more intimate surprise of small geometrical gardens opening off them, rather as the rooms of an enormous house would open off the corridors".{{sfn|Scott-James|1974|p=38}} Nicolson considered the garden's success was down to this "succession of privacies: the forecourt, the first arch, the main court, the tower arch, the lawn, the orchard. All a series of escapes from the world, giving the impression of cumulative escape".{{sfn|Scott-James|1974|p=111}} In the White Garden and along some paths in other gardens, the flower beds were set off from the paths by closely clipped low square hedges of [[Buxus|box]].{{sfn|Lord|1995|pp=145–146}}

[[File:SISSINGHURST CASTLE GARDEN A border with a large Berberis.JPG|thumb|upright=1.2|alt=a flowerbed of mainly white and purple flowers against a brick wall|"Cram, cram, cram, every chink and cranny."<ref name=cram/>]]
Sackville-West's planting philosophy is summed up in the advice from one of her gardening columns in the ''Observer'': "Cram, cram, cram, every chink and cranny".<ref name=cram>{{cite web|url=https://www.houseandgarden.co.uk/article/gardens-in-kent|title=From Sissinghurst to Chartwell – the best gardens to visit in Kent|first=Daisy|last=Allsup|publisher=House & Garden|website=houseandgarden.co.uk|date=13 August 2018|access-date=3 October 2018}}</ref> Gardener Sarah Raven (Adam Nicolson's wife) notes the use of the vertical dimension, as well as horizontal paths, in her planting. Assisted by the number of walls still standing from the [[Tudor period|Tudor]] manor, and constructing more of her own, Sackville-West remarked "I see we are going to have heaps of wall space for climbing things."<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/gardening/gardenstovisit/10770627/Sissinghurst-Vita-Sackville-Wests-lavish-approach-to-gardening.html|title=Sissinghurst: Vita Sackville-West's lavish approach to gardening|first=Sarah|last=Raven|date=18 April 2014|work=The Telegraph|access-date=3 October 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181003181857/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/gardening/gardenstovisit/10770627/Sissinghurst-Vita-Sackville-Wests-lavish-approach-to-gardening.html|archive-date=3 October 2018|url-status=live|ref=none}}</ref>

Old roses formed the centrepiece of the planting, and their history appealed to her as much as their appearance did: "there is nothing scrimpy or stingy about them. They have a generosity which is as desirable in plants as in people", and ultimately around 200 varieties were grown at Sissinghurst.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.countrylife.co.uk/gardens/country-gardens-and-gardening-tips/the-history-of-sissinghursts-roses-58258|title=The History of Sissinghurst's Roses|first=Troy|last=Scott Smith|date=28 June 2014|work=Country Life|access-date=31 October 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180930194013/https://www.countrylife.co.uk/gardens/country-gardens-and-gardening-tips/the-history-of-sissinghursts-roses-58258|archive-date=30 September 2018|url-status=live}}</ref>

====Influences====
[[Edwin Lutyens]], long-time gardening partner of [[Gertrude Jekyll]], was a friend to both Sackville-West and Nicolson and a frequent visitor to Long Barn, and gave advice regarding Sissinghurst.{{sfn|Brown|1982|p=183}}{{efn|[[Christopher Hussey (historian)|Christopher Hussey]] records Lutyens sketching the design for [[The Cenotaph, Whitehall|the Cenotaph]] when at dinner with Vita Sackville-West on the day [[David Lloyd George|Lloyd George]] had awarded him the commission.{{sfn|Hussey|1989|p=392}}}} Sackville-West denied that Jekyll's work had an impact on her own designs, but Nigel Nicolson described Lutyens' influence as "pervasive".{{sfn|Brown|1982|p=183}} Fleming and Gore go further, suggesting that the use of groupings of colours "followed Jekyll"; "a purple border, a cottage garden in red, orange and yellow, a walled garden pink [and] purple, a white garden, a herb garden".{{sfn|Fleming|Gore|1988|p=220}} Scott-James notes however that [[herbaceous borders]], "Jekyll's speciality", were much disliked by Sackville-West.{{sfn|Scott-James|1974|p=41}} Other influencers and friends were the noted plantswoman [[Norah Lindsay]],<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/gardening/3345942/Norah-Lindsay-a-begetter-of-beauty.html|title=Norah Lindsay: a begetter of beauty|first=Stephen|last=Lacey|date=7 December 2007|work=The Telegraph|access-date=11 November 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181111133847/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/gardening/3345942/Norah-Lindsay-a-begetter-of-beauty.html|archive-date=11 November 2018|url-status=live}}</ref> the plant collector [[Collingwood Ingram]], who was their neighbour at [[Benenden]],{{sfn|Scott-James|1974|p=69}} and Reginald Cooper, one of Nicolson's closest friends, whose earlier garden at [[Cothay Manor]] in [[Somerset]] has been described as the "Sissinghurst of the West Country".<ref name="GardenGuide">{{cite web |url=http://www.gardens-guide.com/gardenpages/_0225.htm |title=Cothay Manor Gardens |work=Gardens Guide |access-date=9 December 2008 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130102190236/http://www.gardens-guide.com/gardenpages/_0225.htm |archive-date=2 January 2013 |url-status=live}}</ref> Sackville-West's considerable knowledge of old roses was deepened by her friendship with [[Edward Bunyard]], plantsman, epicure, and the author of ''Old Garden Roses'', who was a frequent visitor.{{sfn|Brown|1985|p=131}} The historian Peter Davey places the garden at the very end of a tradition of [[Arts and Crafts movement|Arts and Crafts gardening]] which by the 1930s, in the face of changes in "taste and economics", had almost come to its close.{{sfn|Davey|1995|p=137}}

{{quote box|width=25em|bgcolor=#c6dbf7|align=left|quote=Formality is often essential to the plan of a garden but never to the arrangement of its flowers and shrubs.|source=–[[William Robinson (gardener)|William Robinson]], author of ''The English Flower Garden'' and a major influence on Sackville-West's planting style{{sfn|Scott-James|1974|p=41}}}}
The concept of "garden rooms" has been dated to the [[Ancient Rome|Romans]], who included rooms within some homes that opened on one side onto a garden. The horticultural scholar and gardener [[Marie-Luise Gothein]] identified such a room at [[Pliny the Younger|Pliny's]] Villa Tusci, in her study ''A History of Garden Art''.{{sfn|Gothein|2014|pp=99–100}} In the late 19th century, reaction set in against both the [[Victorian era|Victorian]] fashion for elaborate [[Bedding (horticulture)|bedding]] and [[Italianate architecture|Italianate]] formality, and the earlier 18th century [[English landscape garden|landscape gardening]] modelled on the paintings of [[Claude Lorrain]] and [[Nicolas Poussin]].{{sfn|Davey|1995|p=125}} This led in part to a concept of the "garden room" (distinct from the architectural concept of a [[sunroom]] as a garden room) as a space out of doors, in which paths, corresponding to halls in a house, lead to enclosed gardens within the garden as a whole, conceived of as rooms. The architect [[Hermann Muthesius]] described the style which developed into the Arts and Crafts approach in his ''{{lang|de|Das englische Haus}}'' ("[[The English House]]"): "the garden is seen as a continuation of the rooms of the house, almost a series of ... outdoor rooms, each of which is self-contained".{{sfn|Davey|1995|p=129}} A number of pre-Sissinghurst gardeners, including Jekyll and Lawrence Johnston, had designed in this style, and much of their work was known to Sackville-West and Nicolson.{{sfn|Scott-James|1974|p=41}}{{sfn|Brown|1985|pp=162–163}} This landscaping feature has since become an established one in garden design.{{sfn|Erler|1999}}

Many of the gardening themes developed at Sissinghurst were conceived during Sackville-West's and Nicolson's time at Long Barn: the prominence of roses,{{sfn|Brown|1985|p=67}} the emphasis on "rectilinear perspectives" through axial paths,{{sfn|Brown|1985|p=72}} and an informal, massed planting approach.{{sfn|Brown|1985|p=103}} Jane Brown suggests that "without Long Barn there would have been no Sissinghurst."{{sfn|Brown|1985|p=75}}

====Top Courtyard and Tower Lawn====
[[File:Sissinghurst Gardens 9 (4907349737).jpg|thumb|upright=1.2|left|alt=a flowerbed of purple flowers against a brick wall|The Purple Border]]
Entered through the archway in the West Range, that had been blocked for over 100 years before Sackville-West and Nicolson's arrival, the Top Courtyard is dominated by the Tower.{{sfn|Nicolson|2008b|p=10}} Planted against a new wall constructed on ancient foundations is the Purple Border, a colour palette deliberately chosen by Sackville-West in defiance of Gertrude Jekyll's dictum against massing purple flowers.{{sfn|Nicolson|2008b|p=11}} The gardening writer [[Tony Lord]] considers it "the courtyard's greatest glory".{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=23}} The height of the Tower attracts considerable wind which necessitates intensive staking of the plants,{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=28}} particularly the taller specimens such as Sackville-West's much-favoured ''[[Rosa moyesii]]''.{{sfn|Raven|2014|p=359}}{{efn|Sackville-West often employed gardening metaphors, once calling her vacillating cousin [[Edward Sackville-West, 5th Baron Sackville|Eddie Sackville-West]] "as floppy as an unstaked [[delphinium]] in a gale".{{sfn|Sackville-West|2010|p=246}}}} On the opposite side of the Tower is the Tower Lawn, also known as the Lower Courtyard; Nicolson emphasised that "the English lawn is the basis of our garden design".{{sfn|Nicolson|2008b|p=10}} The west–east vista from the Top Courtyard, through the Tower gateway, across the Tower Lawn, and to the statue of Dionysus across the moat, forms one of the most important horizontal axes. It bisects the north–south axis running from the White Garden, across the Tower Lawn, to the Roundel in the Rose Garden.{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=35}} In the southwestern corner of the Tower Lawn is a small garden known as the Sunk Garden. It was created in 1930 as the Lion Pond, but the pond was prone to leaking and was drained in 1939.<ref name="auto6"/> The site was subsequently considered for planting what became the White Garden, but was ultimately rejected as too confined, shady, and damp.{{sfn|Raven|2014|p=88}} The Trust is considering reinstatement of the pool.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://sissinghurstcastle.wordpress.com/tag/the-sunk-garden/|title=The Sunk Garden |first=Liz|last=Maynard|date=9 July 2015|work=Sissinghurst Gardeners Blog|access-date=3 December 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181204151658/https://sissinghurstcastle.wordpress.com/tag/the-sunk-garden/|archive-date=4 December 2018|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://moniquewolak.org/lion-pond/?lang=en|title=Lion Pond|first=Monique|last=Wolak|date=17 November 2017|work=Monique Wolak|access-date=3 December 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181205003208/http://moniquewolak.org/lion-pond/?lang=en|archive-date=5 December 2018|url-status=live}}</ref>

====White Garden====
[[File:Sissinghurst Castle Garden - The White Garden - geograph.org.uk - 26686.jpg|thumb|upright=1.2|right|alt=a view of a garden of white flowers with hedging and a boathouse to the right|The White Garden viewed from the Tower]]
"A symphony in subtle shades of white and green",{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=5}} the White Garden is considered the "most renowned" and most influential of all of Sissinghurst's garden rooms.{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=128}} Planned before the war, it was completed in the winter of 1949–1950.{{sfn|Nevins|1984|pp=1332–1339}} Using a palette of white, silver, grey, and green, it has been called "one of Vita and Harold's most beautiful and romantic visions".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/sissinghurst-castle-garden/features/a-moonlit-masterpiece-at-sissinghurst-castle-garden|title=A moonlit masterpiece at Sissinghurst Castle Garden|author=Helen Champion|work=National Trust|access-date=3 October 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181003221011/https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/sissinghurst-castle-garden/features/a-moonlit-masterpiece-at-sissinghurst-castle-garden|archive-date=3 October 2018|url-status=live}}</ref> Sackville-West recorded her original inspiration in a letter to Nicolson dated 12 December 1939: "I have got what I hope will be a lovely scheme for it: all white flowers, with some clumps of very pale pink".{{sfn|Nicolson|1967|p=48}}{{efn|At this point, the plan was to construct the White Garden on the site of the recently drained Lion Pond.{{sfn|Scott-James|1974|p=102}}}} The concept of single-colour gardens had enjoyed some popularity at the end of the 19th century, but few such gardens remained when Sissinghurst was designed. Influences for the White Garden include [[Hidcote Manor Garden|Hidcote]] and Phyllis Reiss's garden at [[Tintinhull Garden|Tintinhull]], both of which Vita had seen.{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=129}} Gertrude Jekyll had discussed the concept, but argued for varying the white palette with the use of blue or yellow plants, advice followed by Reiss. But neither Hidcote nor Tintinhull equals the "full-scale symphony" of the White Garden at Sissinghurst.{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=129}} A more prosaic motivation for the colour scheme was to provide reflected illumination for Sackville-West and Nicolson as they made their way from their bedrooms at the South Cottage to the Priest's House for dinner.{{sfn|Brown|1998|p=127}}
{{quote box|width=25em|bgcolor=#c6dbf7|align=right|quote=For the last 40 years of my life I have broken my back, my fingernails, and sometimes my heart, in the practical pursuit of my favourite occupation.|source=–Sackville-West's reflections on Sissinghurst towards the end of her life<ref name="auto">{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/books/2014/mar/09/vita-sackville-west-sissinghurst-review-raven-gardening|title=Vita Sackville-West's Sissinghurst review – a wealth of inspiration for gardeners|first=Kate|last=Kellaway|date=9 March 2014|work=The Guardian|access-date=26 January 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180930193157/https://www.theguardian.com/books/2014/mar/09/vita-sackville-west-sissinghurst-review-raven-gardening|archive-date=30 September 2018|url-status=live|df=dmy-all}}</ref>}}
The focal point of the garden was originally four almond trees, encased in a canopy of the white rose, [[List of Rosa species|''Rosa mulliganii'']].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/105800/i-Rosa-mulliganii-i-(Ra)/Details|publisher=Royal Horticultural Society|title=Rosa mulliganii (Ra)|access-date=29 October 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181028225855/https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/105800/i-Rosa-mulliganii-i-(Ra)/Details|archive-date=28 October 2018|url-status=live}}</ref> By the 1960s, the weight of the roses had severely weakened the trees, and they were replaced with an iron [[arbor (garden)|arbour]] designed by Nigel Nicolson.{{sfn|Nicolson|2008b|p=32}} Beneath the arbour is sited a [[Ming dynasty]] vase bought in Cairo.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://sissinghurstcastle.wordpress.com/2013/12/13/the-white-garden-rose-rosa-mulliganii/|first=Jo|last=Jones|title=The White Garden Rose (Rosa mulliganii)|date=13 December 2013|work=Sissinghurst Gardeners Blog|access-date=6 October 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181006154957/https://sissinghurstcastle.wordpress.com/2013/12/13/the-white-garden-rose-rosa-mulliganii/|archive-date=6 October 2018|url-status=live}}</ref> A lead statue of a [[Vestal Virgin]], cast by [[Toma Rosandić]] from the wooden original which is in the Big Room, presides over the garden. Sackville-West intended that the statue should be enveloped by a weeping pear tree, ''[[Pyrus salicifolia]]'' 'Pendula', and the present tree was planted after her original was destroyed in the [[Great Storm of 1987]].{{sfn|Brown|1998|pp=126–127}} Lord considers the White Garden "the most ambitious and successful of its time, the most entrancing of its type".{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=147}}

A possibly apocryphal story records a visit by the colour-loving gardener [[Christopher Lloyd (gardener)|Christopher Lloyd]], during which he is supposed to have scattered seeds of brightly coloured [[Tropaeolum|nasturtiums]] across the lawn.{{sfn|Clayton|2013|p=41}} Troy Scott Smith, the current head gardener, is undertaking a major research project on the history of the White Garden with the intention of recreating the original planting scheme in its entirety. This project has seen the number of plants being propagated in the Sissinghurst nursery rise from 400 to over 530.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://sissinghurstcastle.wordpress.com/2014/10/02/plants-of-significance/|title=Plants of Significance|first=Emma|last=Grigg|date=2 October 2014|work=Sissinghurst Gardeners Blog|access-date=11 November 2018}}</ref>

====Rose Garden====
[[File:Formal Gardens at Sissinghurst Castle - geograph.org.uk - 1387062.jpg|thumb|upright=1.2|left|alt=a circular enclosure of green hedging surrounding a lawn|The Roundel in the Rose Garden]]
The Rose Garden was constructed on the site of the old kitchen garden from 1937.{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=46}} It terminates the north–south axis running from the White Garden and concludes with a brick wall, designed by A. R. Powys and known as the Powys Wall, constructed in 1935.<ref name="parksandgardens.org"/> [[Old garden roses]], those bred before 1867, formed the heart of the garden's planting.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.countrylife.co.uk/gardens/country-gardens-and-gardening-tips/the-history-of-sissinghursts-roses-58258|title=The history of Sissinghurst's roses|date=28 June 2014|work=Country Life|access-date=3 October 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180930194013/https://www.countrylife.co.uk/gardens/country-gardens-and-gardening-tips/the-history-of-sissinghursts-roses-58258|archive-date=30 September 2018|url-status=live}}</ref> Such roses appealed not only for their lavish appearance, but also for their history. The informal and unstructured massing of the plants was Sackville-West's deliberate choice, and has become one of Sissinghurst's defining features.{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=47}} Roses were supplied by, among others, [[Hilda Murrell]] of Edwin Murrell Ltd., notable rose growers in [[Shropshire]],{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=47}} and the florist [[Constance Spry]] from her home [[Winkfield Place]].{{sfn|Scott-James|1974|p=104}} In addition to using established suppliers and receiving plants as gifts from friends, Sackville-West sometimes sourced specimens herself. Sarah Raven records Sackville-West digging up the [[hybrid perpetual rose]] 'Souvenir du Docteur Jamain' at an old nursery;{{sfn|Raven|2014|pp=199–200}}{{efn|Sackville-West recounted: "I found him growing against the office wall of an old nursery. No one knew what he was; no one seemed to care; no one knew his name; no one had troubled to propagate him. Could I dig him up, I asked? Well, if you like to risk it, they said, shrugging their shoulders; it's a very old plant, with a woody stiff root. I risked it; ''Docteur Jamain'' survived his removal; and now has a flourishing progeny in my garden."{{sfn|Raven|2014|p=200}}}} Anne Scott-James noted that the rose had passed out of commerce and it was Sackville-West who returned it to cultivation.{{sfn|Scott-James|1974|pp=73–74}} The Rose Garden is divided by the Roundel, constructed of yew hedging by Nicolson and Nigel in 1933.{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=46}} As elsewhere in the garden, the Trust has replaced the original grass paths with stone and brick, to cope with the increases in visitor numbers.{{sfn|Brown|1998|p=76}} Scott-James considered the roses in the Rose Garden "one of the finest collections in the world".{{sfn|Scott-James|1974|p=73}} The writer Jane Brown describes the Rose Garden, more than any other including the White, as expressing "the essence of Vita's gardening personality, just as her writing-room enshrines her poetic ghost".{{sfn|Brown|1998|p=77}}

====Delos and Erechtheum====
Delos, between the Priest's House and the courtyard wall, was the one area of the garden that neither Sackville-West nor Nicolson considered a success.{{sfn|Nicolson|2008b|p=35}} She explained its origins in an article in [[Country Life (magazine)|''Country Life'']] in 1942 as being inspired by the terraced ruins covered with wild flowers she had observed on the island of [[Delos]].{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=147}} Neither the shade nor the soil, nor its inter-relationships with other parts of the garden, have proved satisfactory, either in the Nicolson's time or subsequently.{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=147}} The [[Erechtheion|Erechtheum]], named after one of the temples at the [[Acropolis of Athens|Acropolis]], is a vine-covered [[loggia]] and was used as a place for eating out of doors.{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=128}}

====Cottage and Herb Gardens====
[[File:The South Cottage (geograph 3918264).jpg|thumb|upright=1.2|right|alt=a cottage built of pink brick in the middle of a garden. Spring flowers and two tall Cyprus trees stand in front of the cottage|The South Cottage from the Cottage Garden]]
The dominating colours in the [[Cottage Garden]] are hot saturated shades of red, orange, and yellow,{{sfn|Nicolson|2008b|p=18}} a colour scheme that both Sackville-West and Nicolson claimed as their own conception. Lord considers it as much a traditional "cottage garden as [[Marie Antoinette]] was a milkmaid".{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=76}} Here, as elsewhere, Sackville-West was much influenced by [[William Robinson (gardener)|William Robinson]], a gardener she greatly admired and who had done much to popularise the concept of the cottage garden. It contains four beds, surrounded by simple paths, with planting in colours that Sackville-West described as those of the sunset.{{sfn|Brown|1998|p=99}} Plants include a range of [[dahlias]], a particular favourite of Nicolson's, and the [[Kniphofia|red-hot poker]], which he despised.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.countrylife.co.uk/gardens/the-secrets-of-the-cottage-garden-74431|last=Scott Smith|first=Troy|title=The secrets of the cottage garden|date=1 August 2015|work=Country Life|access-date=3 November 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181103210344/https://www.countrylife.co.uk/gardens/the-secrets-of-the-cottage-garden-74431|archive-date=3 November 2018|url-status=live}}</ref> In a 1937 letter to his wife he observed, "I think the secret of your gardening is simply that you have the courage to abolish ugly or unsuccessful flowers. Except for those beastly red-hot pokers which you have a weakness for, there is not an ugly flower in the whole place."{{sfn|Brown|1985|p=131}}

The Herb Garden contains [[Salvia officinalis|sage]], [[thyme]], [[hyssop]], [[fennel]] and an unusual seat built around a [[camomile]] bush.<ref name="auto1"/> Known to the family as [[Edward the Confessor|Edward the Confessor's]] chair, it was constructed by Copper, the Nicolson's chauffeur.{{sfn|Scott-James|1974|p=100}} Originally laid out in the 1930s, the garden was revitalised by John Vass in the years immediately after the Second World War.{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=110}} The Lion Basin in the centre of the garden was brought back from Turkey in 1914.{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=111}} Most of the over one hundred herbs in the garden are now started in the nurseries and planted out at appropriate times of year.{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=112}}

====Walks, the Nuttery, and the Moat====
[[File:Lime Walk at Sissinghurst - geograph.org.uk - 188844.jpg|thumb|upright=1.2|left|alt=a path of grey flagstones running between an avenue of trees|Nicolson's Lime Walk, which he called "My Life's Work"{{sfn|Brown|1998|p=89}}]]
The Lime Walk, also known as the Spring Garden, was the one part of Sissinghurst where Nicolson undertook the planting as well as the design.{{sfn|Nicolson|2008b|p=16}} He had originally intended a single axis running straight from the Rose Garden, through the Cottage Garden, and then through the Nuttery to the moat, but the topography of the site precluded that. Instead, an angled walk was established in the mid-1930s, and substantially replanted in 1945–1962.{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=66}} Sackville-West was critical of the angularity of the design, comparing it to Platform 5 at [[Charing Cross railway station|Charing Cross station]], but treasured it as her husband's creation. "I walked down the Spring Garden and all your little flowers tore and bit at my heart. I do love you so, Hadji.{{efn|"[[Hajj|Hadji]]", meaning pilgrim, was Sir Arthur Nicolson's nickname for his son which Sackville-West adopted and used throughout their marriage. His nickname for her was "Mar", a diminutive first used by her mother.{{sfn|Rose|2006|p=47}}}} It is quite simple: I do love you so. Just that."{{sfn|Nicolson|2008b|p=16}} The [[Tilia|limes]] are [[pleached]] and the dominant plant is [[Euphorbia epithymoides|''Euphorbia polychroma'' 'Major']].{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=69}} Nicolson kept meticulous gardening records of his efforts in the Lime Walk from 1947 to the late 1950s{{sfn|Brown|1985|p=181}} and, providing consolation after the end of his parliamentary career,{{efn|Nicolson's close contemporary and sometime friend [[Chips Channon]] recorded Nicolson's defeat at the [[1948 Croydon North by-election|Croydon by-election]] in his diary entry for 12–14 March 1948. "Of course that nice silly Harold Nicolson was the worst candidate in living memory. How humiliating for him, though his ridiculous behaviour as the Labour Candidate cannot altogether explain the big swing-over. What can he think? He must hide his bald pink head in shame."{{sfn|Channon|1967|p=422}}}} he described the walk as "My Life's Work".{{sfn|Brown|1998|p=89}}

The Yew Walk runs parallel to the Tower Lawn. Its narrow width has been problematic, and by the late 1960s the yew hedges were failing. Extensive pruning proved successful in revitalising the avenue.{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=37}}

The Nuttery was famed for its carpet of [[Primula|polyanthus]]. Nicolson called it "the loveliest planting scheme in the whole world".{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=90}} Unlike the other gardens, where flowering plants were placed within flower beds, in the Nuttery{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=90}} and the Orchard{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=118}} plants were allowed to spread across lawns as though they were growing in the wild. By the 1960s, the plants were dying, and attempts to improve the soil did not assist. The primrose carpet was replaced in the 1970s by a mixture of woodland flowers and grasses.{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=90}}
[[File:Walk at Sissinghurst Castle Gardens (geograph 2403203).jpg|thumb|upright=1.2|right|alt=a lawn with flower borders on the left and a brick wall with wisteria on the right|The Moat Walk – "the English lawn is the basis of our garden design"{{sfn|Nicolson|2008b|p=10}}]]

The Moat Walk stands on the old bowling green constructed by Sir Richard Baker in the 1560s{{sfn|Nicolson|2008b|p=22}} and his reconstructed moat wall provides the axis.{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=100}}{{efn|Jane Brown suggests it is older, dating from the house of the de Berhams.{{sfn|Brown|1998|p=103}}}} The [[azaleas]] were bought with the £100 Heinemann prize Sackville-West received in 1946 for her last published poem, ''The Land''.{{sfn|Nicolson|2008b|p=22}} The [[wisteria]] were a gift from her mother, [[Victoria Sackville-West, Baroness Sackville|Lady Sackville]], as were the six bronze vases.{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=100}}{{efn|The vases were part of a larger set, commissioned by [[Sir Richard Wallace, 1st Baronet|Sir Richard Wallace]] and copied from originals at [[Palace of Versailles|Versailles]] for his garden at the [[Château de Bagatelle]]. Those at Sissinghurst were inherited by Lady Sackville, and others from the set are located at Lanhydrock and in the [[Wallace Collection]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cornwallgardenstrust.org.uk/the-historic-development-of-the-gardens-at-lanhydrock-cornwall/|title=The Historic Development of the Gardens at Lanhydrock, Cornwall|last=Lovie|first=Jonathan|work=Cornwall Gardens Trust|access-date=31 October 2018}}</ref>}} A bench designed by Lutyens terminates one end of the walk, the other focal point being the statue of Dionysus across the moat.{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=108}} The two arms of the moat that remain from the medieval house are populated by [[goldfish]], [[Carp#As ornamental fish|carp]], and [[golden orfe]].{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=126}}

====Orchard====
The Orchard was an unproductive area of fruit trees when the Nicolsons arrived. The unplanned layout was retained as a contrast to the formality of most of the garden; the fruit trees were paired with climbing roses and the area provided space for the many gifts of plants and trees they received.{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=118}} The rose ''[[Rosa filipes]]'' 'Kiftsgate', a present from Sackville-West's friend and fellow gardener Heather Muir of [[Kiftsgate Court Gardens|Kiftsgate Court]], is one example.{{sfn|Brown|1985|p=163}} This part of the garden suffered particularly severe losses in the [[Great Storm of 1987]] and much replanting has taken place.{{sfn|Nicolson|2008b|p=27}} The Orchard is the setting for two structures planned by Nigel Nicolson and commissioned in memory of his father: the boathouse and the gazebo.{{sfn|Nicolson|2008b|p=26}} The gazebo, of 1969, is by Francis Pym and has a [[candlesnuffer]] roof intended to evoke those of Kentish [[oast house]]s.{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=126}} The boathouse, of timber construction and with [[Tuscan order|Tuscan]] [[colonnades]], dates from 2002 and is by the local architectural firm [[Purcell (architects)|Purcell Miller Tritton]].{{sfn|Newman|2012|pp=544–546}}

==Plants==
[[File:Sissinghurst white garden.jpg|thumb|upright|alt=Photograph of white flowers in a garden. At the top, sprays of flowers hanging from branches are lit from behind. Beneath and behind those flowers are others that are in the shadows.|''Rosa mulliganii'' (at top) grows on an arbour in the White Garden.{{sfn|Lord|1995|pp=130–131, 137, 140–141}}]]

Tony Lord has noted that Sackville-West and Nicolson intended the gardens at Sissinghurst to be a source of personal enjoyment, rather than to be a public garden displaying rare plants.{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=18}} Aside from Sackville-West's interest in collecting and preserving rare varieties of old roses, the other garden plants were selected primarily for their abilities to look good and grow successfully in their intended planting sites, as opposed to assembling a collection of rare plants from around the world. Later, in the 1960s, Pamela Schwerdt and Sibylle Kreutzberger decided to propagate the most successful flowering plant varieties in order to offer them for sale and make them more easily available to amateur gardeners.{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=19}}

===Roses===
The collection of rose varieties at Sissinghurst is considered to be extraordinary as well as to encapsulate Sackville-West's approach to gardening.{{sfn|Scott-James|1974|p=73}}{{sfn|Brown|1998|p=77}} In 1953, John Vass counted 194 rose varieties on the property.<ref>{{cite web|title=Finding Vita's Lost Roses|url=https://sissinghurstcastle.wordpress.com/2014/02/13/finding-vitas-lost-roses/|first=Helen|last=Champion|work=Sissinghurst Gardeners Blog|date=13 February 2014|access-date=16 December 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181217062918/https://sissinghurstcastle.wordpress.com/2014/02/13/finding-vitas-lost-roses/|archive-date=17 December 2018|url-status=live}}</ref>{{efn|Vass retained an annotated copy of the Hilling's nursery catalogue from 1953. His notes recorded that 170 of the roses within it were planted at Sissinghurst and he recalled at least 24 other varieties not mentioned in the catalogue.{{sfn|Scott-James|1974|p=105}}}} A few modern rose varieties are included: the [[Floribunda (rose)|floribunda]] rose [[Rosa Iceberg|'Iceberg']] is planted in the White Garden, having been supplied by Hilda Murrell to supplement plant losses after a hard winter following Sackville-West's death,{{sfn|Lord|1995|pp=130, 135, 138}} and the bright scarlet [[Garden rose#Climbing and rambling|climbing]] [[Hybrid tea rose|hybrid tea]] 'Allen Chandler' grows on each side of the entrance gate to the Top Courtyard.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.gardensillustrated.com/plants/15-roses-from-sissinghurst-castle/|title=15 roses from Sissinghurst Castle|first=Troy|last=Scott Smith|work=Gardens Illustrated|access-date=11 November 2018}}</ref>{{sfn|Lord|1995|pp=32–33}}

What a combination of words! One almost suffocates in their soft depths, as though one sank into a bed of rose-petals, all thorns ideally stripped away."{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=50}}}}}}
{{multiple image|perrow=2|total_width=300|align=left|image2=Mme Alfred Carrière3.1 r.JPG|alt2=A group of loosely petaled white roses with a tint of pale pink, with the flowers at various stages from a closed bud to a fully open flower, green foliage behind.|caption2='Madame Alfred Carrière' was the first rose she planted at Sissinghurst.{{sfn|Raven|2014|p=102}}|image1=Rosa 'Mme Pierre Oger'.jpg|alt1=Close-up photo of a dark pink rose with a cuplike shape.|caption1='Madame Pierre Oger' was one of Sackville-West's favourite roses.{{sfn|Raven|2014|p=202}}|image4=Rosa 'Felicite et Perpetue'.jpg|alt4=Clusters of flat-petaled white roses and deep pink rosebuds with green foliage|caption4='Félicité et Perpétue' is also grown in the Orchard.{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=118}}|image3=Mmeplantier.JPG|alt3=Close-up of a cup-shaped white rose with a bit of green in the centre, with some pale pink rosebuds alongside.|caption3='Madame Plantier' is grown against trees in the Orchard.{{sfn|Thomas|1971|pp=193, 204}}}}

The focus of Sackville-West's collection was, however, on [[species roses]] and old garden varieties.{{sfn|Lord|1995|pp=46–50}} Sackville-West described her love of the old roses, saying that one should "discard the idea that roses must be limited to certain accepted and accustomed colours, and to welcome the less familiar purples and lilacs, and the striped, flaked, mottled variations which recall the old Dutch flower-paintings; to approach them, in fact, with open and unprejudiced eyes, and also with a nose that esteems the true scent of a rose warmed by the sun."{{sfn|Thomas|1971|p=6}} She was especially fond of the [[Garden roses#Bourbons|bourbon roses]] 'Madame Isaac Péreire' (named after one of the two wives of [[Isaac Pereire]]) and 'Madame Pierre Oger'.{{sfn|Raven|2014|p=202}}{{efn|In one of her gardening columns, Sackville-West gave readers advice on maintenance; "the Bourbon roses should not be heavily pruned. Dead and twiggy wood should be cut out. How easy to say and how scratchy to do".{{sfn|Raven|2014|p=202}}}} [[Graham Stuart Thomas]], who helped locate rose varieties for Sissinghurst and advised Sackville-West on the design of the Rose Garden,{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=47}} described 'Madame Isaac Péreire' as "[p]ossibly the most powerfully fragrant of all roses",{{sfn|Thomas|1971|p=197}} and 'Madame Pierre Oger' as having a "formal perfection unique among roses".{{sfn|Thomas|1971|p=198}}

When she first visited the property, Sackville-West came upon a dark red, [[double-flowered]] form of ''[[Rosa gallica]]'' growing wild and apparently dating from earlier plantings there. She eventually planted it in the Orchard, and it is now known as the [[cultivar]] 'Sissinghurst Castle'.{{sfn|Lord|1995|pp=158–159}}<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/43210/i-Rosa-i-Sissinghurst-Castle-(G)/Details|title=Rosa 'Sissinghurst Castle'|publisher=Royal Horticultural Society|date=13 December 2016|access-date=3 November 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181103210328/https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/43210/i-Rosa-i-Sissinghurst-Castle-(G)/Details|archive-date=3 November 2018|url-status=live}}</ref> In 1930, even before the deeds to the property had been signed, she planted the [[noisette rose]] 'Madame Alfred Carrière' on the south face of the South Cottage, making it the first rose she would plant in the gardens.{{sfn|Raven|2014|p=102}}

In the Rose Garden itself, many roses were planted singly, but two deep pink varieties, the bourbon 'Madame Lauriol de Barny' and the [[Garden roses#Damask|damask]] 'La Ville de Bruxelles', were planted closely in groups of three and allowed to grow together, providing focal points on the left and right sides, respectively, of the garden.{{sfn|Lord|1995|pp=54–55}}

In the White Garden, ''Rosa mulliganii'' is trained over an arbour to provide the centrepiece of the design.{{sfn|Lord|1995|pp=130–131, 137, 140–141}} Several varieties are trained to climb up trees in the Orchard. These include [[Rosa 'Albéric Barbier'|'Albéric Barbier']],{{sfn|Raven|2014|p=119}} described by Thomas as "a great favourite" among the hybrids of ''[[Rosa wichuraiana]]''.{{sfn|Thomas|1971|p=126}} Another is 'Félicité et Perpétue', a ''[[Rosa sempervirens]]'' hybrid that was named for the two daughters of the gardener to the [[Louis Philippe I|Duke of Orléans]] in 1827, who were, in turn, named after [[Perpetua and Felicity]].{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=118}} A third is the noisette 'Madame Plantier',{{sfn|Thomas|1971|pp=193, 204}} of which Sackville-West wrote: "I go out and look at her in the moonlight: she gleams, a pear-shaped ghost, contriving to look both matronly and virginal."{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=119}}
