===Trees and hedges===
[[File:SISSINGHURST CASTLE GARDEN The Prospect Tower from the flower borders.JPG|thumb|alt=View of a garden, with a tall green square-edged hedge at the left, a flower bed with white flowers, edged by a closely clipped low hedge, in the foreground, and brick towers in the background|Formal hedges feature prominently in the gardens.]]

For the most part, Sackville-West and Nicolson simply kept the large trees that were already growing on the property, to serve as the major specimens. These included numerous ancient [[Quercus robur|oaks]] that frame many of the individual gardens.{{sfn|Lord|1995|pp=14–15}} The Orchard was made up of apple and pear trees that had been planted long before; Sackville-West and Nicolson decided to keep them and use them as supports for climbing roses.{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=118}} Similarly, the Nuttery consisted entirely of [[Corylus maxima|filberts]] that appear to have been planted around 1900.{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=97}}

Some trees were added to the plantings, notably the limes of the Lime Walk.{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=66}} A bed of ''[[Magnolia liliiflora]]'' 'Nigra' is at the southern end of the Lower Courtyard,{{sfn|Lord|1995|pp=40–41}} and some ''[[Magnolia grandiflora]]'' are on the walls of the Top Courtyard.{{sfn|Lord|1995|pp=29, 33}} A [[Erythrina crista-galli|coral tree]] is in the Lower Courtyard.{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=45}} Some ''[[Malus]]'' and ''[[Prunus]]'' previously in the Rose Garden died out,{{sfn|Lord|1995|pp=61–62}} as have ''[[Robinia pseudoacacia]]'', ''[[Cercidiphyllum japonicum]]'', and ''[[Koelreuteria paniculata]]'' in the Cottage Garden.{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=77}} A [[catalpa]] was planted as a focal point of the Lower Courtyard lawn in 1932, and Nicolson liked to sit beneath it and read, but it died in the 1960s.{{sfn|Lord|1995|pp=36, 38}}

[[Hedge]]s play a critical role in defining the "garden rooms". [[Taxus baccata|Yews]],{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=37}} [[hornbeams]],{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=70}} and box{{sfn|Lord|1995|pp=145–146}} are each used in this way, clipped into formal square-edged rows of various heights. Yews are also pruned into vertical accents that mimic the shape of [[Italian cypress]].{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=78}}

===Named cultivars===
[[File:Pulmonaria officinalis 'Sissinghurst White'.jpg|thumb|left|alt=Photograph of a small plant with tubular white flowers and green leaves spotted with white.|''Pulmonaria'' 'Sissinghurst White']]
In addition to the 'Sissinghurst Castle' rose, multiple other flowering plants have been grown at Sissinghurst and given names honouring the property or the people associated with it. Sackville-West herself had low enthusiasm for naming plants in this way, and she and Nicolson actually dug up and discarded a rose that was named 'Lady Sackville' after her mother.{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=158}} There are numerous plants that have been given trade names based on the gardens, including ''[[Tanacetum parthenium]]'' 'Rowallane' which has often been mislabelled as 'Sissinghurst',{{sfn|Lord|1995|pp=138–139}} but there are several that are grown at or were discovered at Sissinghurst and were named to reflect the association.

Sackville-West made an exception to her dislike of naming plants in memory of people and purchased [[Viola (plant)|''Viola'']] 'Lady Sackville' late in her life, around 1960, planting it in the Delos. A few years after her death, a seedling appeared that seems to have been a spontaneous cross between 'Lady Sackville' and the variety 'Nellie Britton' that was growing alongside it. It had flowers of a rich pink that were larger than those of the parent varieties. The gardeners named it 'Vita'.{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=159}} Sackville-West had also grown a variety of [[rosemary]] (''Rosmarinus officinalis'') that self-seeded in the Tower steps, and differed from the common variety in having upright rather than trailing stems, and flowers of a deeper shade of blue. It has come to be recognized as a distinct cultivar, and named 'Sissinghurst Blue'.{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=159}}<ref>{{cite web|publisher=Royal Horticultural Society|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/57929/Rosmarinus-officinalis-Sissinghurst-Blue/Details|title=Rosmarinus officinalis 'Sissinghurst Blue'|date=13 December 2016|access-date=3 November 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181103210213/https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/57929/Rosmarinus-officinalis-Sissinghurst-Blue/Details|archive-date=3 November 2018|url-status=live}}</ref>

{{quote box|width=25em|bgcolor=#c6dbf7|align=right|quote=
She walks among the loveliness she made,<br />Between the apple-blossom and the water –<br />She walks among the patterned pied brocade,<br />Each flower her son and every tree her daughter.|source=–Extract from Sackville-West's poem ''The Land'', printed on the service sheet for her funeral {{hsp}}{{sfn|Scott-James|1974|p=113}}}}

In 1969, a gardener in Kent bred a cultivar of [[dwarf bearded iris]] with reddish-purple flowers. He gave a specimen to Sissinghurst, where it was planted in the Purple Border, and named ''Iris'' 'Sissinghurst'.{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=158}} During the 1970s, a pink-flowered specimen of ''[[Glandularia]]'' (''[[Verbena]]'') was given to the garden and named 'Sissinghurst'.{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=159}}<ref>{{cite web|publisher=Royal Horticultural Society|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/353905/i-Glandularia-i-Sissinghurst/Details|title=Glandularia 'Sissinghurst'|date=13 December 2016|access-date=3 November 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181103210325/https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/353905/i-Glandularia-i-Sissinghurst/Details|archive-date=3 November 2018|url-status=live}}</ref> In 1976, the garden was given a distinctive specimen of ''[[Pulmonaria officinalis]]'' that, unlike the species, has large white flowers (along with the white-spotted leaves of the species). It was planted in the White Garden and named 'Sissinghurst White'.{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=158}}{{sfn|Armitage|1989|p=871}}<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/137190/i-Pulmonaria-i-Sissinghurst-White/Details|title=Pulmonaria 'Sissinghurst White'|publisher=Royal Horticultural Society|date=13 December 2016|access-date=3 November 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180924033749/https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/137190/i-Pulmonaria-i-Sissinghurst-White/Details|archive-date=24 September 2018|url-status=live}}</ref> Around 1977, the gardeners purchased a collection of seedlings of ''[[Thalictrum aquilegiifolium]]''. They selected the best plant, having larger flowers, and propagated it. This plant was added to the White Garden and named 'White Cloud'.{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=159}} From a planting of ''Penstemon'' 'Evelyn', which is a selection of ''[[Penstemon barbatus]]'',{{sfn|Armitage|1989|pp=802–803}} a specimen was named 'Sissinghurst Pink', although Lord does not consider it to be distinct from 'Evelyn'.{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=158}}<ref>{{cite web|publisher=Royal Horticultural Society|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/42948/i-Penstemon-i-Sissinghurst-Pink/Details|title=Penstemon 'Sissinghurst Pink'|date=13 December 2016|access-date=3 November 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181103210648/https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/42948/i-Penstemon-i-Sissinghurst-Pink/Details|archive-date=3 November 2018|url-status=live}}</ref>

In the late 1980s, Pamela Schwerdt and Sibylle Kreutzberger found a specimen of ''[[Phlox stolonifera]]'' with a remarkably rich purple colour in a florist's shop near the [[Chelsea Flower Show]]. They planted it in the Top Courtyard and named it 'Violet Vere' after Schwerdt's mother, who had been President of the [[Wild Flower Society (UK)|Wild Flower Society]] and was celebrating her ninetieth birthday.{{sfn|Lord|1995|p=158}}<ref>{{cite web|url=https://plantheritage.wordpress.com/2017/05/03/rare-plant-of-the-month-may-2017/|title=Rare plant of the month, May 2017: ''Phlox stolonifera'' 'Violet Vere'|work=Plant Heritage|date=3 May 2017|access-date=18 December 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181219134224/https://plantheritage.wordpress.com/2017/05/03/rare-plant-of-the-month-may-2017/|archive-date=19 December 2018|url-status=live}}</ref>

'''Ightham Mote''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|aɪ|t|əm|_|ˈ|m|oʊ|t}}), at [[Ightham]], is a medieval moated [[manor house]] in [[Kent]], England. The architectural writer [[Pevsner Architectural Guides|John Newman]] describes it as "the most complete small medieval manor house in the county".{{sfn|Newman|2012|p=320}}  

Ightham Mote and its gardens are owned by the [[National Trust]] and are open to the public. The house is a [[Grade I listed building]], and parts of it are a [[Scheduled Ancient Monument]].

==History==

===14th century–16th century===

The origins of the house date from circa 1340–1360.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1362410 |title=IGHTHAM MOTE - 1362410 |publisher=Historic England |date=1952-08-01 |access-date=2017-03-16}}</ref> The earliest recorded owner is Sir Thomas Cawne, who fought in France with Edward the Black Prince and who acquired the Mote in the 1360s.<ref name="Ightham">''Ightham at the Crossroads'' by Jean Stirk and David Williams published by Red Court Publishing, copyright Ightham Parish Council, Jean Stirk and David Williams, 2015. ISBN 978-0-9930828-0-1</ref>{{sfn|Newman|2012|p=320}} He died in 1374 and there is a memorial to him in St Peter’s Church. In 1399 on the death of his son Robert the house passed by the marriage of Robert’s daughter Alice to [[Nicholas Haute]] and their descendants, their grandson Richard Haute being Sheriff of Kent in the late 15th century.{{sfn|Newman|2012|p=320}} It was then purchased in 1521 by the courtier Sir [[Richard Clement (died 1538)|Richard Clement]] (d.1538).{{sfn|Newman|2012|p=320}} In 1591, Sir [[William Selby (died 1612)|William Selby]] bought the estate.{{sfn|Newman|2012|p=320}}

===16th century-late 19th century===
[[File:Ightham Mote Palmer.jpg|thumb|Ightham Mote c.1828, brownwash painting by Samuel Palmer. Note that part of the building had been converted to an oast house.]]
The house remained in the [[Selby family]] for nearly 300 years.{{sfn|Nicolson|1998|p=38}} Sir William was succeeded by his nephew, also [[William Selby (died 1638)|Sir William]], who is notable for handing over the keys of [[Berwick-upon-Tweed]] to [[James VI and I|James I]] on his way south to succeed to the throne.{{sfn|Nicolson|1998|p=39}}  He married Dorothy Bonham of [[West Malling]] but had no children. The Selbys continued until the mid-19th century when the line faltered with Elizabeth Selby, the widow of a Thomas who disinherited his only son.{{sfn|Nicolson|1998|p=40}} During her reclusive tenure, [[Joseph Nash]] drew the house for his multi-volume illustrated history ''Mansions of England in the Olden Time'', published in the 1840s.{{sfn|Nicolson|1998|p=41}} A brownwash watercolour painting dated c.1828 by [[Samuel Palmer]] shows that part of the building had been converted to an [[oast house]].{{sfn|Grattan|2021|p=119}}

The house passed to a cousin, [[Prideaux John Selby]], a distinguished naturalist, sportsman and scientist. On his death in 1867 he left the house to his daughter Lewis Marianne Bigge. Her second husband, Robert Luard (with whom she had two children, including the organist [[Bertram Luard-Selby]], who had been born at Ightham Mote), changed his name to Luard-Selby. Ightham Mote was rented in 1887 to the American railway magnate [[William Jackson Palmer]] and his family and for three years became a centre for artists and writers of the [[Aesthetic Movement]], with visitors including [[John Singer Sargent]], [[Henry James]] and [[Ellen Terry]]. When Mrs Bigge died in 1889, the executors of her son Charles Selby-Bigge, a [[Shropshire]] land agent, put the house up for sale in July 1889.{{sfn|Nicolson|1998|p=41}}

===Late 19th century-21st century===

The Mote was purchased in 1889 by [[Colyer-Fergusson baronets|Sir Thomas Colyer-Fergusson]].{{sfn|Nicolson|1998|p=41}} He and his wife brought up their six children at the Mote. In 1890–1891, he carried out much repair and restoration, which allowed the survival of the house after centuries of neglect.{{sfn|Nicolson|1998|p=42}}  Ightham Mote was opened to the public one afternoon a week in the early 20th century.{{sfn|Nicolson|1998|p=42}}

Sir Thomas Colyer-Fergusson's third son, [[Thomas Riversdale Colyer-Fergusson|Riversdale]], died aged 21 in 1917 at the [[Battle of Passchendaele|Third Battle of Ypres]], and was awarded a [[Posthumous award|posthumous]] [[Victoria Cross]]. A wooden cross in the New Chapel is in his memory. The oldest brother, Max, was killed at the age of 49 in a bombing raid on an army driving school near [[Tidworth]] in 1940 during [[World War II]]. One of the three daughters, Mary (called Polly) married [[Walter Monckton]].

On Sir Thomas's death in 1951, the property and the baronetcy passed to Max's son, James. The high costs of upkeep and repair of the house led him to sell the house and auction most of the contents.  The sale took place in October 1951 and lasted three days. It was suggested that the house be demolished to harvest the lead on the roofs, or that it be divided into flats.  Three local men purchased the house: William Durling, John Goodwin and John Baldock. They paid £5,500 for the freehold, in the hope of being able to secure the future of the house.{{sfn|Nicolson|1998|p=45}}
 
In 1953, Ightham Mote was purchased by Charles Henry Robinson, an American of [[Portland, Maine|Portland]], [[Maine]], United States. He had known the property from vacations in England during the 1920s, and many years later happened to see the house for sale in ''[[Country Life (magazine)|Country Life]]''.  He lived there for only fourteen weeks a year for tax reasons.  He made many urgent repairs, and partly refurnished the house with 17th-century English pieces. In 1965, he announced that he would give Ightham Mote and its contents to the National Trust. He died in 1985 and his ashes were immured just outside the crypt. The National Trust took possession in that year.{{sfn|Nicolson|1998|p=45}}

In 1989, the National Trust began an ambitious conservation project that involved dismantling much of the building and recording its construction methods before rebuilding it. During this process, the effects of centuries of ageing, weathering, and the destructive effect of the [[deathwatch beetle]] were highlighted. The project ended in 2004 after revealing numerous examples of structural and ornamental features which had been covered up by later additions.{{sfn|Newman|2012|p=320}}

==Architecture and description==
[[Image:IMote.jpg|thumb|left|Ightham Mote: the gatehouse rebuilt in the 1480s]]
Originally dating to around 1320, the building is important because it has most of its original features; successive owners effected relatively few changes to the main structure, after the completion of the quadrangle with a new chapel in the 16th century. [[Pevsner Architectural Guides|Pevsner]] described it as "the most complete small medieval manor house in the county", and it remains an example that shows how such houses would have looked in the [[Middle Ages]]. Unlike most courtyard houses of its type which have had a range demolished so that the house looks outward, Nicholas Cooper observes that Ightham Mote wholly surrounds its courtyard and looks inward, into it, offering little information externally.{{sfn|Cooper|1999|p=65}} The construction is of "Kentish [[ragstone]] and dull red brick,"{{sfn|Cook|1984|p=41}} the buildings of the courtyard having originally been built of timber and subsequently rebuilt in stone.{{sfn|Wood|1996|p=155}}

[[Image:Ightham Mote Moat.JPG|right|thumb|250px|The moat of Ightham Mote]]
The house has more than 70 rooms, all arranged around a central courtyard, "the confines circumscribed by the moat."{{sfn|Cook|1984|p=41}} The house is surrounded on all sides by a square [[moat]], crossed by three bridges. The earliest surviving evidence is for a house of the early 14th century, with the [[great hall]], to which were attached, at the high, or dais end, the [[chapel]], [[crypt]] and two [[solar (room)|solar]]s. The courtyard was completely enclosed by increments on its restricted moated site, and the battlemented tower was constructed in the 15th century. Very little of the 14th century survives on the exterior behind rebuilding and refacing of the 15th and 16th centuries.
 
The structures include unusual and distinctive elements, such as the porter's squint, a narrow slit in the wall designed to enable a gatekeeper to examine a visitor's credentials before opening the gate. An open loggia with a fifteenth-century gallery above, connects the main accommodations with the gatehouse range. The courtyard contains a large, 19th century dog kennel.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1362410 |title=IGHTHAM MOTE - 1362410 |publisher=Historic England |date=1952-08-01 |access-date=2017-03-18}}</ref> The house contains two chapels; the New Chapel, of c.1520, having a barrel roof decorated with [[Tudor rose]]s. {{sfn|Wood|1996|p=240}} Parts of the interior were remodelled by [[Richard Norman Shaw]].<ref>{{cite web|author=Good Stuff |url=http://www.britishlistedbuildings.co.uk/101362410-ightham-mote-ightham#.WMzy1JJFd9A |title=Ightham Mote, Ightham, Kent |publisher=Britishlistedbuildings.co.uk |date=1952-08-01 |access-date=2017-03-18}}</ref>

== In literature ==
Much of [[Anya Seton]]'s novel ''[[Green Darkness]]'' takes place at Ightham Mote. The novel was inspired by a visit Seton made in 1968. Charles Henry Robinson allowed Seton to access his library and notes for research.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Seton |first=Anya |title=Green darkness. |date=1972 |publisher=Hodder and Stoughton |isbn=0-340-15979-0 |location=London |oclc=2722421}}</ref>

1183849.title: Scotney Castle
1183849.extract:
Scotney Castle is an English country house with formal gardens south-east of Lamberhurst in the valley of the River Bewl in Kent, England. It belongs to the National Trust.
The gardens, which are a Site of Special Scientific Interest and a celebrated example of the picturesque style, are open to the public. The central feature is the ruins of a medieval, moated manor house, Scotney Old Castle, which is on an island on a small lake. The lake is surrounded by sloping, wooded gardens with fine collections of rhododendrons, azaleas and kalmia for spring colour, summer wisteria and roses, and spectacular autumn colour.
At the top of the garden stands a house which was built to replace the Old Castle between 1835 and 1843. This is known as Scotney New Castle, or simply Scotney Castle, and was designed by Anthony Salvin. It is an early and unusually restrained example of Tudor Revival architectural style in 19th-century Britain. Following the death of the resident, Elizabeth Hussey, in 2006, this house was opened to the public for the first time on 6 June 2007.

It belongs to the [[National Trust]]. [[Scotney Castle SSSI|The gardens]], which are a [[Site of Special Scientific Interest]] and a celebrated example of the [[picturesque]] style, are open to the public. The central feature is the ruins of a [[medieval]], [[moat]]ed [[manor house]], Scotney Old Castle, which is on an island on a small lake. The lake is surrounded by sloping, wooded gardens with fine collections of [[rhododendron]]s, [[azalea]]s and [[kalmia]] for spring colour, summer [[wisteria]] and [[rose]]s, and spectacular autumn colour. At the top of the garden stands a house which was built to replace the Old Castle between 1835 and 1843. This is known as Scotney New Castle, or simply Scotney Castle, and was designed by [[Anthony Salvin]]. It is an early and unusually restrained example of [[Tudor Revival]] [[architectural style]] in 19th-century Britain. Following the death of the resident, Elizabeth Hussey,Mrs. Hussey, a daughter of Member of Parliament [[Peter Kerr-Smiley]] and his wife, the former Maud Simpson, was at one time a niece by marriage to [[Wallis Warfield]], later the [[Duchess of Windsor]]. in 2006, this house was opened to the public for the first time on 6 June 2007. ==Location== Scotney Castle is located in South East England, in the county of Kent. Nearby settlements are [[Lamberhurst]] and [[Kilndown]], however the nearest large town is [[Royal Tunbridge Wells]] {{convert|3.5|miles}} away. Although the A21 main road passes the grounds, it cannot be seen from the Castle. ==History== [[File:Scotney Castle aerial view.jpg|thumb|left|Aerial view of the castle]] [[File:scotney-wyrdlight-1136.jpg|thumb|Scotney 'New' Castle]] [[File:scotney-wyrdlight-1140.jpg|thumb|Scotney 'New' Castle]] [[File:scotney-wyrdlight-1150.jpg|thumb|Scotney 'New' Castle]] [[File:Scotney Castles.jpg|thumb|upright|right|A photograph of the old (foreground) and new castles]] The earliest record from 1137 gives the owner of the estate as Lambert de Scoteni. Roger Ashburnham is credited with building the [[castle]] c.1378–80. Construction of the castle began as a roughly rectangular fortified house with towers in each corner. The original plan may never have been finished, and by 1558 it is likely only the southern tower remained. In 1580 the south wing was rebuilt in [[Elizabethan architecture]] style, and around 1630 the eastern range was rebuilt in three-story [[Inigo Jones]] style. The Elizabethan wing remained a bailiff's residence until 1905, but the eastern range was partly dismantled on the completion of the new house in 1843, leaving the ruin as a garden feature. The [[Recusant]] owner [[Thomas Darrell]] hid [[Jesuit]] Father [[Richard Blount, S.J.]] in the castle while he ministered to [[Roman Catholics]] from 1591 to 1598. Catholicism was then illegal in England, and during the second raid by authorities to arrest the priest he fled over a wall into the moat and escaped. The Darrell family owned the estate for some 350 years. In 1778 [[Edward Hussey (cricketer)|Edward Hussey]] bought the estate and his grandson, also Edward, built the 'new' Castle to the designs of [[Anthony Salvin]], from sandstone quarried from the slope below. The hollow created was developed into a Quarry Garden and contains a 100-million-year-old impression of a [[dinosaur]]'s footprint. On [[Christopher Hussey (historian)|Christopher Hussey]]'s death in 1970 the estate was left to the [[National Trust]]. Several apartments in the castle and on the estate were let out by the Trust, with tenants including Prime Minister [[Margaret Thatcher]] who rented the Belfry flat for a time during the 1970s and 1980s, when it served as a weekend escape for her from Westminster life.[https://archive.today/20130505113646/http://www.thisiskent.co.uk/Iron-Lady-lived-doorstep/story-12010470-detail/story.html%23axzz2QWsNqtcM When the Iron Lady lived on our doorstep], This is Kent, 18 February 2011
[https://news.bbc.co.uk/local/kent/hi/front_page/newsid_9404000/9404762.stm Margaret Thatcher's Lamberhurst bolthole], BBC News, 23 February 2011 When her husband [[Denis Thatcher]] was made a [[Thatcher baronetcy|baronet]] in 1990, his new title was gazetted with the [[territorial designation]] ''of Scotney in the County of Kent''.{{London Gazette |issue=52443 |date=7 February 1991 |page=1993}} The castle grounds have played host to [[Shakespeare]] productions, notably ''[[A Midsummer Night's Dream]]'', with the actors appearing from behind the bushes on cue. Old Scotney Castle was used as the location for the video to the Squeeze song ''[[Some Fantastic Place (song)|Some Fantastic Place]]''. ==See also== * [[Castles in Great Britain and Ireland]] * [[List of castles in England]] ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== {{Commons category|Scotney Castle}} *[https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/scotney-castle Scotney Castle information at the National Trust] *[https://web.archive.org/web/20041212163102/http://www.theheritagetrail.co.uk/castles/scotney%20castle.htm A comprehensive history of Scotney Castle] {{Authority control}} {{Coord|51.0928|0.4082|display=title|region:GB|format=dms}} [[Category:Country houses in Kent]] [[Category:Gardens in Kent]] [[Category:National Trust properties in Kent]] [[Category:Historic house museums in Kent]] [[Category:Buildings and structures in the Borough of Tunbridge Wells]] [[Category:Anthony Salvin buildings]] [[Category:Grade I listed buildings in Kent]] [[Category:Anthony Salvin]] [[Category:Grade I listed parks and gardens in Kent]] [[Category:Prime ministerial homes in the United Kingdom]]

1448351.title: Oldbury Camp
1448351.extract: Oldbury Camp (also known as Oldbury hill fort) is the largest Iron Age hill fort in south-eastern England. It was built in the 1st century BC by Celtic British tribes on a hilltop west of Ightham, Kent, in a strategic location overlooking routes through the Kentish Weald. The fort comprises a bank and ditch enclosing an area of about 50 hectares (120 acres), with entrances at the north-east and south ends. Wooden gates barred the entrances. Archaeological excavations carried out in the 1930s and 1980s found that the hill fort's interior had probably not been permanently occupied. It had been abandoned around 50 BC and the north-east gate had been burned down, possibly due to a Roman invasion. The wooded southern part of Oldbury Camp is now owned and managed by the National Trust and is open to the public.

{{Short description|Hillfort in Kent, England}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=April 2022}}
[[File:Ramparts on the Southwest of Oldbury Hillfort, Kent.jpg|right|thumb|Bank on the southwestern ramparts of the hillfort]]
'''Oldbury Camp''' (also known as '''Oldbury hill fort''') is the largest [[Iron Age]] [[hill fort]] in south-eastern [[England]].<ref name="DarvillStamper2002" /> It was built in the 1st century BC by [[Celtic Britons|Celtic British]] tribes on a hilltop west of [[Ightham]], [[Kent]], in a strategic location overlooking routes through the Kentish [[Weald]]. The fort comprises a bank and ditch enclosing an area of about {{convert|50|ha}}, with entrances at the north-east and south ends. Wooden gates barred the entrances. Archaeological excavations carried out in the 1930s and 1980s found that the hill fort's interior had probably not been permanently occupied. It had been abandoned around 50 BC and the north-east gate had been burned down, possibly due to a Roman invasion. The wooded southern part of Oldbury Camp is now owned and managed by the [[National Trust]] and is open to the public.

==Description==
[[File:Oldbury Camp OS map.png|right|thumb|upright|Ordnance Survey map of Oldbury Camp]]
Oldbury Camp is located near the village of Ightham, Kent. It is situated on the summit of Oldbury Hill, a partly wooded plateau on a north–south alignment on the [[Greensand Ridge]]. It is bounded by very steep natural cliffs on the eastern side, with commanding views over one of the main routes through the Weald. The hill fort covers an area of around {{convert|50|ha}} and is of the [[multivallate]] type; while its defences mostly comprise a single bank and ditch surrounding the north, west and south of the hilltop, in a few places the bank is doubled to provide extra defences. The bank probably originally stood about {{convert|10|m}} high, though it survives only to a height of about {{convert|1|m}}, while the ditch is up to {{convert|3.5|m}} wide and is situated about {{convert|3|m}} below the bank's crest.<ref name="NHLE" />

At least two entrances were constructed, on the north-east and southern ends of the hill fort.<ref name="Dyer1981">{{cite book|last=Dyer|first=James|title=The Penguin guide to prehistoric England and Wales|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=zmeBAAAAMAAJ|year=1981|publisher=Penguin|page=183}}</ref> A spring is located near the centre of the site and would have ensured a constant supply of fresh water for the hill fort's defenders. Overhangs and hollows in the rocks on the eastern side of the hill fort were occupied as long ago as the [[Middle Palaeolithic]] period and are now known as the [[Oldbury rock shelters]].<ref name="DarvillStamper2002">{{cite book|last1=Darvill|first1=Timothy|last2=Stamper|first2=Paul|last3=Timby|first3=Jane|title=England: An Oxford Archaeological Guide to Sites from Earliest Times to AD 1600|url=https://archive.org/details/oxfordarchaeolog00timo|url-access=registration|year=2002|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-284101-8|pages=[https://archive.org/details/oxfordarchaeolog00timo/page/353 353]–5}}</ref>

==History==

The hill fort was constructed during the first century BC, likely in a rapidly executed project carried out on a massive scale.<ref name="Pastscape" /> Around 100 BC, a V-shaped ditch about {{convert|1.5|m}} deep was initially cut to form the outer perimeter of Oldbury Camp and the spoil was heaped up to form a bank.<ref name="Dyer1981" /> The defences follow a rough diamond shape, measuring {{convert|1350|m}} north-south by {{convert|700|m}} east-west.<ref name="NHLE">{{NHLE|num=1007458|desc=Large multivallate hillfort and Palaeolithic rock shelters at Oldbury Hill|access-date=28 April 2017}}</ref> The eastern side above the cliffs was probably defended only by a wooden [[pallisade]], as the cliffs there made it unnecessary to continue the bank and ditch along the escarpment.<ref name="Pastscape">{{PastScape|mname=Oldbury Camp|mnumber=409479|access-date=28 April 2011}}</ref>

[[File:Northern Bank on Oldbury Hillfort.jpg|thumb|left|The northern bank of the hillfort]]

The defences were subsequently strengthened by adding further material to the bank to create a [[glacis]]. The ditch was widened to give it a wide, flat bottom of the [[Fécamp]] type, named after a Gaulish ''[[oppidum]]'' near the eponymous town in [[Normandy]]. A stone [[revetment]] was constructed at the north-east entrance, probably with a wooden [[breastwork (fortification)|breastwork]], above and beside a heavy wooden gate protected by a defensive [[outwork]]. The gate was destroyed by burning and a large quantity of [[Sling (weapon)|sling]] stones was found nearby. Another gate was constructed at the south entrance but has been badly damaged by the construction of a modern road. It is not clear whether buildings existed in the hill fort's interior, although large quantities of pottery have been discovered there.<ref name="Dyer1981" /> Oldbury Camp was probably used only as a temporary shelter or a place of refuge, rather than as the site of a permanent settlement.<ref name="NT-history" />

The reasons for the construction and eventual abandonment of Oldbury Camp are unclear, but it may have been built by a local tribe seeking to resist the invasion at the time of the [[Belgae]], a tribal confederation from northern [[Gaul]]. They were evidently unsuccessful as the Belgae conquered and settled in Kent. The fort was abandoned around the time of [[Caesar's invasions of Britain]] in 55 and 54 BC and may have been attacked by the Romans, if the burned northern gate indicates an assault rather than [[slighting]] by retreating defenders.<ref name="NT-history">{{cite web|url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/oldbury-hill/features/oldbury-hill-kent--an-iron-age-hillfort|title=Oldbury Hill, Kent – an Iron Age Hillfort|publisher=National Trust|access-date=27 April 2017}}</ref> Parts of the site appear to have been reused for quarrying during the Roman period.<ref name="NHLE" />

==Excavations==

Oldbury Camp has been excavated archaeologically twice: once in 1938 by [[John Bryan Ward-Perkins]] and again in 1983–84. While the 1938 excavations suggested that the hill fort had been built in two phases about half a century apart, this theory was abandoned as a result of the 1983–84 excavations determining that it was instead constructed as a single rapidly executed project. It had previously been thought that modifications to the defences were the result of the Belgae refortifying it against the Roman invasion but this now seems unlikely.<ref name="Pastscape" />

==Access==

[[File:Pathway through the southern half of Oldbury Wood.jpg|thumb|right|The southern half of the interior of the hillfort is now forested and under the ownership of the National Trust]]

The southern part of Oldbury Hill and Styants Wood immediately to the west is now in the ownership of the National Trust, which acquired it in 1945, and is open to the public. It is managed by [[Kent County Council]].<ref name="Pastscape" /> The northern part is privately owned farmland, but is covenanted to protect it.<ref name="Dyer1973">{{cite book|last=Dyer|first=James|title=Southern England: an archaeological guide: the prehistoric and Roman remains|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=dU5nAAAAMAAJ|year=1973|publisher=Noyes Press|isbn=978-0-8155-5016-7|pages=208–9}}</ref>

6735776.title: Old Soar Manor
6735776.extract:
Old Soar Manor is an English Heritage property, owned and maintained by the National Trust. Located near Plaxtol, Kent, England, it is a small 13th century stone manor house. It is listed Grade I on the National Heritage List for England.
Built in 1290, the manor originally belonged to the Culpepper family. The centre of the house was originally the great hall but this no longer exists, as it was demolished in 1780 and replaced with the red-brick farmhouse on the site. The farmhouse is Grade II listed.  Visitors today can see the solar, latrine and chapel which remain.

It was originally called Spiers but renamed in honour of Wolfe's death and victory at the Battle of Quebec in 1759. [[File:Quebec House, Quebec Square, Westerham, Kent - geograph.org.uk - 1296826.jpg|300px|thumb|Quebec House]]
'''Quebec House''' is the birthplace of General [[James Wolfe]] on what is now known as Quebec Square in [[Westerham]], [[Kent]], England. The house is [[Listed building#England and Wales|listed Grade I]] on the [[National Heritage List for England]] since September 1954.<ref name=NHLE>{{NHLE|num=1244133|desc=Quebec House|access-date=14 April 2019|mode=cs2}}</ref>

The house dates from the mid 16th century but much of the current appearance is from the 1630s. It was originally called Spiers but renamed in honour of Wolfe's death and victory at the [[Battle of the Plains of Abraham|Battle of Quebec]] in 1759. The house is now owned by the [[National Trust]] and open to the public with paintings and memorabilia relating to Wolfe's life.

==History==
Originally called Spiers, the house was built between 1530 and 1550 as a timber-framed L-shaped building.<ref name=hist/> It was altered in the 1630s, when the current exterior was added.<ref name=hist/><ref name=NHLE/>

[[James Wolfe]] was the son of a distinguished general, [[Edward Wolfe]] who rented Spiers.<ref>{{cite book |title=General Wolfe |last=Salmon |first=Edward |date=1909 |publisher=Cassell & Company |series=Makers of National History |editor-first=W. H. |editor-last=Hutton |pages=1–2 |url=https://archive.org/stream/generalwolfe00salmuoft#page/2/mode/2up |access-date=8 March 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161009044245/https://archive.org/stream/generalwolfe00salmuoft#page/2/mode/2up |archive-date=9 October 2016|url-status=live }}</ref> Wolfe lived there from 1728 until 1738.<ref>{{cite web |title=Lieut. General James Wolfe, |url=http://theweald.org/N10.asp?NId=2198 |publisher=The Weald |access-date=8 March 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190822022355/http://theweald.org/N10.asp?NId=2198 |archive-date=22 August 2019 |url-status=live }}</ref>

The house was renamed after his victory at the [[Battle of Quebec (1759)|Battle of Quebec]].<ref name=hist>{{cite web |title=History at Quebec House |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/quebec-house/features/history-at-quebec-house |publisher=National Trust |access-date=8 March 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171208054827/https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/quebec-house/features/history-at-quebec-house |archive-date=8 December 2017 |url-status=live }}</ref> It was occupied in 1911 by Canadian author [[Henry Beckles Willson]] and his family.<ref>1911 England Census</ref> Joseph Bowles Learmont of Montreal acquired the house and presented it to the [[National Trust]] in 1917.<ref name=NHLE/>

==Architecture and contents==

The square brick building has two storeys and an attic with a tiled pitched roof. The three-[[Bay (architecture)|bay]] front has three equal gables. There is a water pump by the back door which dates from 1792.<ref name=NHLE/>  A blue plaque along the outer brick wall marks the entrance of the Wolfe's home.<ref>{{cite web |title=General James Wolfe, Quebec House, Westerham, Kent. UK |url=https://www.waymarking.com/waymarks/WMJ6M8_General_James_Wolfe_Quebec_House_Westerham_Kent_UK |publisher=Waymarking |access-date=8 March 2020}}</ref>

Various pictures relating to the life of General Wolfe are displayed in the house.<ref>{{cite web |title=National Trust, Quebec House |url=https://www.artuk.org/visit/venues/national-trust-quebec-house-7462 |publisher=Art UK |access-date=8 March 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160612115335/http://artuk.org/visit/venues/national-trust-quebec-house-7462 |archive-date=12 June 2016 |url-status=live }}</ref> The purchase of two portraits was assisted by the [[Art Fund]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Quebec House |url=https://www.artfund.org/whats-on/museums-and-galleries/quebec-house |publisher=Art Fund |access-date=8 March 2020 |archive-date=26 September 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200926081437/https://www.artfund.org/whats-on/museums-and-galleries/quebec-house |url-status=dead }}</ref>

The house is surrounded by a garden stocked with plants which would have been available in the 18th century.<ref name="explore">{{cite web |title=Explore Quebec House |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/quebec-house/features/things-to-see-and-do-at-quebec-house |publisher=National Trust |access-date=8 March 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171208054721/https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/quebec-house/features/things-to-see-and-do-at-quebec-house |archive-date=8 December 2017 |url-status=live }}</ref> The coach house has been converted into a tea room and bookshop with an exhibition on the battle and on Wolfe's life. The house itself contains memorabilia and paintings connected to him.<ref name="explore"/>

'''Smallhythe Place''' in [[Small Hythe]], near [[Tenterden]] in [[Kent]], is a [[Timber framing|half-timbered]] house built in the late 15th or early 16th century and since 1947 cared for by the [[National Trust]]. It was the home of the [[Victorian era|Victorian]] actress [[Ellen Terry]] from 1899 to her death in the house on 17 July 1928.{{sfn|Kazmier|2001|p=174}} The house contains Ellen Terry's theatre collection, while the cottage grounds include her rose garden, orchard, nuttery and the working Barn Theatre.{{sfn|Patton|2004|p=60}}

==Early history==
The design of the house appears to be from the early 16th century and may have been built after a fire in the village of Small Hythe in 1514.{{sfn|Smallhythe Place's history}} The house was originally called 'Port House' and before the [[River Rother, East Sussex|River Rother]] and the sea receded it was associated with the nearby thriving shipyard{{sfn|Melville|1997|p=34}} – in [[Old English]] ''hythe'' means "landing place". Changes to the flow of the Rother led to the silting-up of the channel and, eventually, the decline of the industry.{{efn|A 1998 [[Time Team]] archaeological dig uncovered evidence of the historic shipbuilding industry, leading to creation of a new monument classification - Deserted Medieval Shipyard.{{sfn|The Port Community of Smallhythe}}{{sfn|Bellamy|Milne|2017}}}} The estate subsequently converted to agriculture after the late 17th century, at which point the barn was erected. The barn likely served as storage for both animals and crops, and was expanded during the 19th century.{{sfn|Smallhythe Place's history}}

==Terry's residence==
Terry first saw the house in 1890{{sfn|Patton|2004|p=58}} in the company of [[Henry Irving]],{{sfn|Melville|1997|p=34}} the manager of the [[Lyceum Theatre, London|Lyceum Theatre]] in London's [[Covent Garden]], with whom she shared a famous theatrical partnership for nearly 24 years.{{sfn|Kazmier|2001|p=172}} She expressed interest in buying the property, but was unable to do so until 1899 when it became available.{{sfn|Patton|2004|p=58}} The property comprised two cottages (one of which, called the Priest's House, she gave to her daughter{{sfn|Oram|2011|p=201}}) and a barn.{{sfn|Melville|1997|p=34}} 

Terry lived in the house for the last 3 decades of her life and it served as a place to relax in between a busy schedule of theatre engagements and international travel.{{sfn|Melville|1997|p=34}} Terry entertained friends there but also relished the time spent caring for her gardens. Her daughter suggested the transformation of the barn into a theatre, but Terry preferred to retain the isolated nature of the estate.{{sfn|Smallhythe Place's history}}

==The museum==
[[File:The bedroom, Smallhythe Place.jpg|thumb|alt=The bedroom of a Tudor cottage, decorated with antique furniture|Ellen Terry's bedroom]]
The house was opened to the public by Terry's daughter [[Edith Craig]] in 1929, as a memorial to her mother, showcasing both personal mementos as well as letters collected from a national appeal after her mother's death.{{sfn|Rank|2021|pp=40-42}}  The [[National Trust]] supported Craig in her running of the museum from 1939,{{sfn|Patton|2004|p=60}} and took over the property when she died in 1947.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Oram |first=Alison |title=Prejudice and Pride: LGBTQ and its contemporary implications |publisher=Research Centre for Museums and Galleries, School of Museum Studies, University of Leicester |year=2018 |isbn=978-1-898489-50-4 |editor-last=Sandell |editor-first=Richard |pages=57–62 |language=English |chapter=Pride of Place: Valuing, mapping and curating queer heritage |editor-last2=Lennon |editor-first2=Rachael |editor-last3=Smith |editor-first3=Matt}}</ref> It was designated as a Grade II* [[listed building]] by [[English Heritage]] on 8 May 1950.<ref>[http://www.britishlistedbuildings.co.uk/101071163-smallhythe-place-tenterden#.WRiG61TTWhA "Smallhythe Place"], British Listed Buildings, accessed 14 May 2017.</ref>

Smallhythe Place contains many personal and theatrical mementos, including two walls devoted to [[David Garrick]] and [[Sarah Siddons]]. Other exhibits include a message from [[Sarah Bernhardt]] displayed in the Dining Room,{{sfn|Isaac|2018|p=27}} a chain worn by [[Fanny Kemble]], Sir [[Arthur Sullivan]]'s monocle and a visiting card from [[Alexandre Dumas]]. There are also several paintings by the artist [[Clare Atwood]], one of the romantic companions of Edith Craig.{{sfn|Oram|2011|p=198}} In the Terry Room (previously used as a sitting room) is a letter from [[Oscar Wilde]] begging Terry to accept a copy of his first play.{{sfn|Isaac|2018|p=24}} The bedroom remains largely as it was during Terry's lifetime,{{sfn|Smallhythe Place's history}} while the library contains over 3000 volumes, largely those collected by Terry and used during her career.{{sfn|Isaac|2018|p=34-35}}

==The Ellen Terry Costume Collection==
In addition to a wealth of personal ephemera, Smallhythe Place also hosts an archive of Terry's role in the [[Aestheticism|Aesthetic Movement]] and the role she played in the design of her stage wardrobe.{{sfn|Isaac|2012|p=94}} The Costume Room displays a selection of sumptuous costumes dating from Terry's time at the [[Lyceum Theatre, London|Lyceum Theatre]], in particular three costumes from Henry Irving's spectacular production of ''[[Much Ado About Nothing]]'' at the Lyceum Theatre{{sfn|Patton|2004|p=60}} and the iridescent beetle-wing dress she wore as [[Lady Macbeth]] in 1888{{sfn|Lynch|2022|p=24}} designed by [[Alice Comyns Carr]].{{sfn|Isaac|2012|p=101}} The dress was returned to public display in 2011 after 1300 hours of conservation.{{sfn|PR Newswire|2011}}

==Barn Theatre==
[[File:The Barn Theatre, Smallhythe Place.jpg|thumb|alt=The interior of a large wooden barn, which has been converted to a theatre, with a view of the stage and two rows of wooden chairs|The interior of the Barn Theatre]]
In 1929, Craig finally did establish a [[barn theatre]] in the house's grounds.{{sfn|Smallhythe Place's history}} The 70-seat theatre hosts around 30 productions a year.<ref name=Brown>{{cite web |last = Brown |first = Mark |title = Joanna Lumley pays tribute to method acting forerunner Ellen Terry |publisher = The Guardian |date = March 4, 2020 |url = https://www.theguardian.com/stage/2020/mar/04/joanna-lumley-pays-tribute-to-method-acting-forerunner-ellen-terry |accessdate = July 7, 2021}}</ref>

Every year since 1929 on the anniversary of Ellen Terry's death there has been a tradition of performing the plays of [[William Shakespeare]].{{sfn|Smallhythe Place's history}} 
Among the actors who have performed in the theatre have been [[Peggy Ashcroft]], [[Edith Evans]], [[John Gielgud]], [[Alec Guinness]], [[Nigel Hawthorne]], [[Rachel Kempson]], [[Michael Redgrave]], [[Paul Scofield]] and [[Sybil Thorndike]].<ref name=NT1>{{cite web |title= Joanna Lumley: Patron of the Barn Theatre |publisher= National Trust |url= https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/smallhythe-place/features/joanna-lumley-patron-of-the-barn-theatre |accessdate= July 7, 2021}}</ref>

The first patron of the Barn Theatre was Ellen Terry's great-nephew Sir John Gielgud, who served in the role for 50 years before being succeeded by [[Donald Sinden]], who was patron for 20 years until his death in 2014. He was succeeded by [[Joanna Lumley]], who took up the role in March 2020.<ref name=Brown/><ref name=NT1/>

'''Owletts''' is a [[country house]] {{convert|1.3|km|mi|1|order=flip}} to the northwest of the village of [[Cobham, Kent|Cobham]] in Kent, England.

It is a [[Grade II*]] listed building owned by the [[National Trust]].<ref name=listed>{{cite web |url =http://www.britishlistedbuildings.co.uk/en-356759-owletts-cobham-kent |title =Owletts, Cobham |website =www.britishlistedbuildings.co.uk |accessdate=11 December 2013 }}</ref><ref>{{NHLE |num =1049097 |desc=Owletts, The Street |accessdate=12 December 2013 }}</ref>

==History==
The house was originally built in 1683–84 for Bonham Hayes (died 1720), a successful, yeoman farmer of the Cobham area, and his wife Elizabeth.<ref name=Newman>{{cite book |first=John |last=Newman |title=The buildings of England: Kent - West and the Weald |date=2012 |publisher=Yale |page=194 |edition=3}}</ref>
The red-brick Kentish [[Yeoman]]'s house is symmetrical, two storeys high, with sliding sash and [[dormer]] windows. The house interiors date in part to 1684, and include a remarkably ornate [[Restoration style|Carolean plasterwork]] ceiling above the principal staircase.<ref name=express>{{cite web |url =http://www.britainexpress.com/attractions.htm?attraction=3676 |title =Owletts |website =www.britainexpress.com |accessdate=12 December 2013 }}</ref>

Having passed to Hayes's son, Richard, then his grandson (also Richard),<ref name=Newman/> the house passed in 1894 to the Edmeades family of [[Nurstead]] (also in the parish of [[Gravesend, Kent|Gravesend]]), then by marriage to the Baker family.<ref name=listed/>

In 1862 the renowned architect [[Herbert Baker|Sir Herbert Baker]] was born here. Owletts became Herbert Baker's home in later life and he made numerous alterations including the addition of a porch and a wing on the north-west corner of the house.  He also removed the wall between the entrance hall and the drawing room and in that room installed an ornamental 'Empire' clock.<ref name=listed/>  The family filled the house with specially commissioned or collected furniture.<ref name=express/>

The house has a garden partly designed by [[Gertrude Jekyll]], who was introduced to Baker by [[Edwin Lutyens]] (her friend) when he was working with Baker in [[Ernest George]] and [[Harold Peto]]'s architectural office in London.<ref>{{cite web |url =http://www.artefacts.co.za/main/Buildings/archframes.php?archid=60 |title =BAKER, Sir Herbert John |website =www.artefacts.co.za |accessdate=12 December 2013 }}</ref>

[[Acanthus (plant)|Acanthus]] plants growing in the garden are symbolic of Herbert Baker's architectural profession.  Also within the garden is a bird-bath formed from Tivoli Order variant [[Corinthian order|Corinthian capitals]] salvaged from the old [[Bank of England]] building by [[John Soane]] when Sir Herbert rebuilt the Bank (between 1925 and 1939).<ref>{{cite web |url =http://www.bankofengland.co.uk/education/Pages/museum/walkthrough/buildings.aspx |title =Buildings and Architects |website =www.bankofengland.co.uk |accessdate=12 December 2013 }}</ref>

When Herbert Baker died at the age of 83 on 4 February 1946 he left Owletts to the National Trust.<ref>{{cite journal |year=1942 |title=Herbert Baker |journal=[[The Round Table: The Commonwealth Journal of International Affairs]]  |volume=36 |issue=142 |pages=107–108  |doi=10.1080/00358534608451375}}</ref>  The National Trust lets the property, but some rooms and the garden are opened regularly to the public.  The last tenant was David Baker, the great-grandson and heir of Sir Herbert Baker, who lived there together with his family until the rent was increased in 2023. A petition was begun to keep the house open to the public. 

The National Trust have said it will open ‘for at least 2 days’ a year but no new tenant is yet in place.<ref>{{Cite news |last= |first= |date=2023-10-18 |title=Family ‘forced out’ of country house left to National Trust |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2023/10/18/national-trust-owletts-sir-herbert-baker-family-forced-out/ |access-date=2024-06-12 |work=The Telegraph |language=en-GB |issn=0307-1235}}</ref>

The house closed in 2011 for a £1 million refit, during which the collection of 900 objects and 1,400 books was carefully packed and stored off-site.<ref>{{cite web |url =http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/article-1356393500748/ |title =Returning the historic collection at Owletts |website =www.nationaltrust.org.uk |accessdate=12 December 2011}}</ref> It reopened on 7 April 2013.<ref>{{cite news |first=Anna |last=Dubuis |date=14 January 2013 |title=Sir Herbert Baker's Cobham house Owletts to reopen |url=http://www.gravesendreporter.co.uk/news/sir_herbert_baker_s_cobham_house_owletts_to_reopen_1_1791737 |newspaper=The Reporter |location=Gravesend  }}</ref>

56647572.title: One Tree Hill and Bitchet Common
56647572.extract:
One Tree Hill and Bitchet Common is a 79.2-hectare (196-acre) biological Site of Special Scientific Interest east of Sevenoaks in Kent. It is in Kent Downs Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty and One Tree Hill is managed by the National Trust
This site has mixed woodland on the Lower Greensand, some of it of ancient origin. The habitats are varied, including acidic soils on Bitchet Common and damp, base-rich soils in Martins Wood. There are several rare plants and invertebrates.
The site is in several blocks crossed by public footpaths.
